\chapter*{How to use the reference catalogue}
\addcontentsline{toc}{chapter}{How to use the reference catalogue}
This catalogue is a reference work for institutional quantitative research. Its four parts separate foundations and research methods; portfolio, pricing and trading methods; markets and instruments; and data, systems and research resources. Chapters bring foundations, implementation references and recent research together by subject. A work or explicitly identified version has one primary home; links connect its other applications.

For a selected sequence, use the separate \href{institutional_quantitative_finance_learning_guide.pdf}{learning guide}. Its overview routes and sequenced specialist pathways specify required readings, prerequisites, outcomes and replication checkpoints. Specialist readings connect contract mechanics, valuation, evidence, data and implementation without a fixed reading-count cap. \emph{Core} means required for one of those routes; catalogue inclusion alone is not a priority ranking.

Each entry separates \textbf{difficulty}, \textbf{resource type} and \textbf{publication/version status}. Intro assumes mathematical maturity but no specialism; Intermediate bridges introductory and specialist material; Advanced assumes graduate methods or market knowledge; Research denotes specialist work. ``Not specified'' is used where the inherited entry gives no defensible level. Type describes the resource, and status records the selected edition, date, draft or living documentation. An unspecified date is not a claim of currency. Paired works and editions retain their separate names and version qualifications within the same primary entry.

Default annotations describe contribution and applicability. Longer qualifications are available through an entry's \emph{Extended note} link in the companion HTML file. Keep that file and both PDFs together when sharing them. Entries retain searchable identifiers, and chapter/section links support browsing without a prescribed reading order. Version-record links expose publication dates, selected revisions, verification scope, version relationships and a review policy for every entry. Inherited metadata is labelled separately from dated source inspections, including the 12 October 2026 crypto-roadmap enhancement; unknown fields remain explicit. This is not an exhaustive external-source or legal-currentness clearance.

Underlying assets, legal instruments, pooled vehicles and strategies describe different layers. A wrapper, label or region does not establish an independent source of diversification. Read contract, cash-flow, data, financing and implementation references together. Working papers, bounded case studies and restricted data retain their limitations. Unresolved leads and intentional exclusions remain in the editorial records, outside the recommended readings.
\part{Foundations and research methods}
\chapter{Mathematics, probability and statistics}\label{catalogue-chapter-1}
Calculus and linear algebra support introductory probability; proof-based analysis supports measure theory and graduate inference. Different texts offer alternative treatments, not a compulsory sequence.

\section{Theoretical, Bayesian and nonparametric statistics}\label{catalogue-section-1-3}

\section{High-dimensional statistics and random matrices}\label{catalogue-section-1-hd}
Large panels and many signals require non-asymptotic and random-matrix tools. Read these before covariance shrinkage, factor-count selection and high-dimensional portfolio tests.

\section{Heavy tails, extremes and dependence}\label{catalogue-section-1-tails}
Tail estimation, extreme-value theory and copulas underpin stress calibration, tail-risk hedging, catastrophe pricing and default dependence. Small tail samples make model uncertainty part of the result.

\section{Stochastic control, BSDEs and mean-field games}\label{catalogue-section-1-control}
Dynamic programming, viscosity solutions and backward SDEs connect portfolio choice, execution, market making and nonlinear pricing. Mean-field games describe many interacting traders.

\EntryRecency{exp-koijen-yogo-demand-system}{Inherited publication/version chronology (date roles retained): Journal of Political Economy 127(4), 1475–1515, August 2019; published online 19 June 2019; DOI 10.1086/701683.}{Journal of Political Economy 127(4), 1475--1515, August 2019; published online 19 June 2019; DOI 10.1086/701683.}{2026-10-04 (inherited metadata evidence; not a fresh source check in this expansion)}{Inherited metadata screen for selected linked sources. \ExtendedNote{exp-koijen-yogo-demand-system}{Models heterogeneous institutional and household demand from portfolio holdings and asset characteristics, using an instrumental-variable approach to address the price--demand endogeneity. It supplies an equilibrium foundation for asking how crowding, investor mandates, and reallocations change prices and strategy capacity, before reading the newer quantitative-investment elasticity estimates. The empirical application is US equities: inferred demand curves depend on holdings coverage, instruments, and investor aggregation, and are not a direct trade-level impact or capacity measure for every asset class.}

\section{Econometrics and time series}\label{catalogue-section-2-2}
\label{sec:s7-forecast}
Regression and inference are prerequisites. Financial forecasting references, including \hyperlink{s7-tsay}{Tsay}, \hyperlink{s7-hamilton}{Hamilton} and \hyperlink{s7-hyndman}{Hyndman--Athanasopoulos}, appear in Section~\ref{sec:s7-forecast}.
Physical-measure volatility forecasts and implied-surface pricing answer different questions; see Section~\ref{sec:derivatives} for pricing and hedging references.

\section{Forecasting models and benchmarks}\label{catalogue-section-2-3}
\label{sec:exp-forecasting}
\ExtendedNote{subject-96}{Foundation models are likely to be more reliable initially for auxiliary forecasts---volatility, volume, spread, demand, curve dynamics and risk scenarios---than for raw excess returns. These targets offer denser signal, clearer scoring rules and greater opportunity to incorporate known covariates. TimesFM's current open release supports a 16,000-step context and quantile forecasts, but the repository explicitly notes that the open version is not an officially supported Google product, which matters for production governance. \sourcecite{23}}
\href{catalogue_extended_notes.html\#subject-96}{Subject context and qualifications}.
\ExtendedNote{subject-97}{Read with the Chronos, TimesFM and transformer entries. The useful comparison is against appropriately trained statistical and simple ML baselines on the same information set, horizon and loss; broad benchmark rank alone is not financial alpha.}
\href{catalogue_extended_notes.html\#subject-97}{Subject context and qualifications}.

\ExtendedNote{exp-domain-benchmarks}{Argues that pooled forecasting leaderboards can hide domain-specific failures and illustrates the problem with comparisons across financial and nonfinancial datasets. It provides a recent counterweight to model-release claims: sampling frequency, missingness, stochastic dynamics and concept drift change what a forecast benchmark measures. Use it to organise auxiliary forecasts such as volume or volatility separately from return prediction, with metrics chosen for each decision. This position paper motivates domain-aware evaluation; its benchmark comparisons do not establish tradable financial performance or a preferred model for every desk.}

\ExtendedNote{exp-moirai}{Introduces Moirai, a pretrained forecasting transformer designed for mixed frequencies, variable-dimensional multivariate series, and varying distributions across a large cross-domain archive. It offers a useful comparison with the catalogue's Chronos and TimesFM entries when testing zero-shot forecasts for curves, macro releases, volumes, and volatility. A general-domain benchmark win is not evidence of return alpha; finance tests should use disjoint temporal holdouts, realistic covariate release times, regime splits, and probabilistic calibration. Check whether each target series appeared in pretraining before claiming zero-shot validity.}

\section{Event studies and long-run abnormal returns}\label{catalogue-section-2-events}
Design and inference for short- and long-horizon event studies: normal-return models, event-induced variance, cross-correlation of clustered events, characteristic-matched benchmarks and calendar-time tests. The Kothari--Warner survey and the Lyon--Barber--Tsai and Fama (1998) papers are in Section~\ref{catalogue-section-10-events}.

Warner, \href{https://doi.org/10.1016/0304-405x(85)90042-x}{``Using daily stock returns''}}{Advanced}{Research paper}{Journal of Financial Economics, 14(1), 3--31 (1985); DOI 10.1016/0304-405x(85)90042-x.}{Examines how the properties of daily returns affect event-study methods. Daily data present few difficulties: standard market-model procedures are usually well specified even when daily features are ignored, though allowing for autocorrelation and event-induced variance can help, and tests that ignore cross-sectional dependence can be well specified and more powerful. Extends the authors' 1980 monthly-data study.}{}

\section{Standard errors, clustering and weak instruments}\label{catalogue-section-2-inference}
Inference for regressions on financial panels and time series: heteroskedasticity- and autocorrelation-robust covariance estimators, one-way, two-way and design-based clustering, predictive-regression bias, and weak instruments. Newey--West (1987) and nonstandard errors are in Section~\ref{catalogue-section-5-2}.

The starting point for every robust and clustered standard error used in finance.}{}

\chapter{Machine learning and alternative data}\label{catalogue-chapter-3}
Separate predictive modelling from asset-pricing claims. Compare flexible models with simple baselines, and track dependence, missingness, data availability and model selection.

\section{Financial learning and alpha research}\label{catalogue-section-3-2}
\label{sec:exp-alpha-ml}
Read with Gu--Kelly--Xiu, Nagel and the factor-model references. These papers connect statistical learning limits and economic restrictions to dynamic portfolio objectives; the complexity critique supplies an explicit counterpoint to the random-feature result.

\CatalogueEntry{exp-seemingly-virtuous-complexity}{Stefan Nagel, \href{https://www.nber.org/papers/w34104}{Seemingly Virtuous Complexity in Return Prediction}}{Research}{Research paper}{NBER Working Paper 34104, August 2025; author lists a July 2025 revision; no journal publication established as of 4 October 2026.}{Analyzes the random-Fourier-feature setting behind the catalogue's Kelly--Malamud--Zhou complexity reading. When features vastly outnumber a short training window, the forecast reduces to a similarity-weighted average of recent returns, effectively a volatility-timed momentum rule; artificial reversal data exposes that inductive bias. Reproduce the simple implied rule and test alternative return regimes before attributing performance to learned economic structure; the critique targets the stated short-window setting, not all nonlinear ML.}{\href{catalogue_extended_notes.html\#exp-seemingly-virtuous-complexity}{Extended note}.}

\ExtendedNote{exp-seemingly-virtuous-complexity}{Analyzes the random-Fourier-feature setting behind the catalogue's Kelly--Malamud--Zhou complexity reading. When features vastly outnumber a short training window, the forecast reduces to a similarity-weighted average of recent returns, effectively a volatility-timed momentum rule; artificial reversal data exposes that inductive bias. This makes it a rare mechanism check on an apparently successful complex forecaster. Reproduce the simple implied rule and test alternative return regimes before attributing performance to learned economic structure; the critique targets the stated short-window setting, not all nonlinear ML.}

\section{Graph and relational models}\label{catalogue-section-3-3}
\ExtendedNote{subject-98}{Graph models are most defensible when edges have an economically auditable meaning---supplier--customer relationships, common ownership, index membership, derivatives linkages, collateral networks or blockchain transfers. Fully learned graphs may improve forecasting loss while making exposure, turnover and failure modes difficult to explain.}
\href{catalogue_extended_notes.html\#subject-98}{Subject context and qualifications}.

\ExtendedNote{exp-missing-financial-data}{Shows that missing firm fundamentals are widespread and structured rather than isolated random holes; the paper proposes an imputation approach using both time and cross-sectional dependence. For institutional characteristic panels, missingness may encode firm size, reporting policy, and coverage, so naïve complete-case screens or global median fills can change factor premia and portfolio composition. Use it to define explicit missing-data diagnostics and compare imputed, missing-indicator, and observed-only strategies. Any imputation used for live forecasts must be fitted using only information available at the decision date.}
\CatalogueEntry{exp-missing-pricing-panels}{Joachim Freyberger, Bjoern Hoeppner, Andreas Neuhierl, and Michael Weber, \href{https://doi.org/10.1093/rfs/hhae003}{Missing Data in Asset Pricing Panels}}{Research}{Research paper}{The Review of Financial Studies 38(3), 760--802, March 2025 issue; published online 27 January 2024.}{Develops conditional-mean imputation and weighted least squares inside a GMM framework so asset-pricing panels can retain return observations with partly missing predictors and still support valid inference under the paper's assumptions. It complements Bryzgalova et al., which focuses on the structure and reconstruction of missing fundamentals. Historical panel validity does not by itself guarantee that the imputed feature existed at a live decision time.}{\href{catalogue_extended_notes.html\#exp-missing-pricing-panels}{Extended note}.}

\ExtendedNote{exp-missing-pricing-panels}{Develops conditional-mean imputation and weighted least squares inside a GMM framework so asset-pricing panels can retain return observations with partly missing predictors and still support valid inference under the paper's assumptions. Historical panel validity does not by itself guarantee that the imputed feature existed at a live decision time.}

\ExtendedNote{exp-financial-data-value}{Develops a sufficient-statistics approach to the private value of financial data using equilibrium return moments and other investors' information demand. It clarifies why a dataset's value depends on the investor's portfolio, competitors, information type, and market liquidity, even when the raw feed is identical. Use it to frame procurement around incremental decision value and expected capacity, not a vendor's claim of unique predictive content. The model is an economic valuation framework; actual license fees, historical reconstruction costs, and marginal execution value still require an institution-specific pilot.}

\ExtendedNote{exp-loughran-mcdonald}{Demonstrates that generic sentiment dictionaries misread finance vocabulary and builds finance-specific word lists using 10-K filings. It is the essential transparent baseline before claiming that FinBERT or an LLM extracts incremental signal from reports, conference calls, or news. An institutional replication should freeze dictionary version, parsing, filing timestamps, amendments, and the mapping from text to tradable entity. Tone associations with market outcomes are neither causal effects nor proof of a durable post-cost strategy.}

\ExtendedNote{exp-bloomberggpt}{Describes a finance-specific 50-billion-parameter language model trained on both proprietary financial text and general corpora, with evaluation on financial and general NLP tasks. It is useful for understanding domain pretraining, benchmark selection, and the limits of comparing proprietary text models with open baselines. Its reported task scores do not establish an investable signal, and the proprietary training corpus limits independent contamination and reproducibility checks. Use a point-in-time model/data cutoff and explicit downstream economic tests before financial forecasting claims.}

\ExtendedNote{exp-llm-econometrics}{Separates using an LLM to predict future outcomes from using it to measure a textual construct for downstream inference. For prediction, it requires no training leakage into the evaluated sample; for measurement, a human-labeled validation sample is needed to quantify model/prompt errors and produce defensible inference. This is the natural governance companion to financial LLM alpha papers: freeze model version and training cutoff, create a genuinely forward test, and validate the extracted labels. Merely prompting a model to 'ignore future information' does not remove knowledge already learned during pretraining.}

\section{Generative models and scenarios}\label{catalogue-section-3-6}
\ExtendedNote{subject-103}{A minimum institutional validation battery for synthetic market data should include unconditional and conditional return distributions, volatility clustering, leverage effects, autocorrelation at multiple transformations, cross-sectional and tail dependence, drawdown duration, regime transitions, order-flow and spread dynamics where applicable, and performance of downstream hedging or execution policies on real holdout data. Privacy or visual realism alone is not enough.}
\href{catalogue_extended_notes.html\#subject-103}{Subject context and qualifications}.

It is a useful baseline for synthetic market paths, but matching marginal distributions and discriminator scores is insufficient without tail, dependence and downstream-policy tests.}{\textit{Applications:} Multi-asset scenarios, simulator training. }

\chapter{Causal inference and experimental design}\label{catalogue-chapter-4}
Start with the estimand and identification assumptions. Platform interference, adaptive policies and trading feedback require more than a conventional independent-unit experiment.
\Needspace{13\baselineskip}
\section{Identification and causal learning}\label{catalogue-section-4-1}
\label{sec:causal}
\label{sec:causal-foundations}
\ExtendedNote{subject-101}{For return prediction, causal ML is most credible when a recognisable intervention, instrument or quasi-experiment exists. Applying causal forests to a panel of endogenous characteristics and returns does not, by itself, identify what would happen if a portfolio manager ``treated'' a security.}
\href{catalogue_extended_notes.html\#subject-101}{Subject context and qualifications}.

\ExtendedNote{exp-policy-learning-observational}{Uses doubly robust value estimates to learn constrained treatment-assignment rules from observational data when an identification strategy is available. It is a rigorous bridge from the catalogue's causal forests and double machine learning to an actual decision policy for execution routing, quote experiments, or client offers. Separate estimation of heterogeneous effects from the choice of action under costs, budget, and capacity constraints. Historical trade or quote logs need overlap, defensible treatment assignment assumptions, and an interference assessment before the learned policy's value can be interpreted causally.}

\ExtendedNote{subject-125}{The lending bibliography in Section~\ref{sec:lending-research-readings} covers supply, search, fee dispersion, lender information and borrow fragility. Distinguish observed demand and predictive rate sensitivity from a causally identified response to pricing. The methods below cover interference, temporal assignment, precision, sequential inference, delayed outcomes and adaptive policy evaluation. Lending applications are methodological extensions, not evidence of a common cross-asset experiment.}

\chapter{Research validation and reproducibility}\label{catalogue-chapter-5}
Read design, selection and replication together. A significant forecast, an implementable strategy and a reproducible experiment are different claims.

\ExtendedNote{exp-model-confidence-set}{Provides a set of forecasting models that can include the best model at a chosen confidence level, making uncertainty across close competitors explicit instead of crowning the smallest observed loss. This extends the catalogue's Diebold--Mariano pairwise test and Hansen's superior-predictive-ability test into a practical model-comparison workflow. Use the same point-in-time holdout and predeclared loss function for all models, with dependence-aware resampling. The confidence set is conditional on the candidate family and evaluation sample; repeated tuning against it invalidates its interpretation.}
\ExtendedNote{exp-nonstandard-errors}{Shows that analyst choices create an evidence-generation uncertainty beyond ordinary sampling error: 164 teams analyzed the same finance data and produced materially different estimates. For an institutional research queue, this motivates independent implementations, explicit specification choices, and a review record before a backtest is treated as a stable finding. Its peer-review stages reduced variation, suggesting practical value in challenge sessions. The experiment measures variation in a particular multi-team design, not a universal adjustment that can be added mechanically to any strategy's standard error.}

\ExtendedNote{latest-conformal-time-dependence}{The incremental question is the validity of a familiar calibration procedure when exchangeability fails, rather than another forecasting architecture. \ExtendedNote{exp-adaptive-conformal}{Adapts conformal prediction-set calibration online as the data-generating distribution shifts, with a long-run coverage-frequency guarantee under the paper's update scheme. It is useful for monitoring volatility, liquidity, or return-prediction intervals after a regime change when static holdout calibration decays. A desk should report realized coverage by horizon, asset group, and stress state alongside interval width. Long-run average coverage is not the same as conditional coverage during a crash, so risk limits need separate tail and path stress.}

\section{Replication and implementability}\label{catalogue-section-5-3}
\label{sec:exp-replication}
Read the papers as a comparison of definitions, samples and statistical designs. Apparently conflicting replication findings can reflect weighting, microcaps, missing data and different null hypotheses; net implementability is a further question.
\CatalogueEntry{exp-replicating-anomalies}{Kewei Hou, Chen Xue, and Lu Zhang, \href{https://doi.org/10.1093/rfs/hhy131}{Replicating Anomalies}}{Research}{Research paper}{The Review of Financial Studies 33(5), 2019--2133, May 2020; first published online 10 December 2018.}{Rebuilds a library of 452 reported cross-sectional anomalies using common portfolio conventions, NYSE breakpoints, and value-weighted returns; most fail even a single-test hurdle under those choices. This is a diagnostic for microcap dependence, inconsistent original implementations, and the difference between a published return spread and an investable portfolio. Pair with Chen--Zimmermann and Jensen--Kelly--Pedersen, which apply different replication definitions and reach more favorable conclusions.}{\href{catalogue_extended_notes.html\#exp-replicating-anomalies}{Extended note}.}

\ExtendedNote{exp-replicating-anomalies}{Rebuilds a library of 452 reported cross-sectional anomalies using common portfolio conventions, NYSE breakpoints, and value-weighted returns; most fail even a single-test hurdle under those choices. This is a diagnostic for microcap dependence, inconsistent original implementations, and the difference between a published return spread and an investable portfolio. \section{Costs, constraints and dynamic trading}\label{catalogue-section-6-2}
\label{sec:exp-portfolio-implementation}

\CatalogueEntry{exp-jagannathan-ma-constraints}{Ravi Jagannathan and Tongshu Ma; correction by Ravi Jagannathan, Tongshu Ma, and Jiaqi Zhang, \href{https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/1540-6261.00580}{Risk Reduction in Large Portfolios: Why Imposing the Wrong Constraints Helps; A Note on ‘Risk Reduction in Large Portfolios: Why Imposing the Wrong Constraints Helps’}; \href{https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/jofi.12824}{2019 published correction}}{Advanced}{Research paper}{The Journal of Finance 58(4), 1651--1683, August 2003, DOI 10.1111/1540-6261.00580; correction in The Journal of Finance 74(5), 2689--2696, October 2019, DOI 10.1111/jofi.12824.}{Shows why nonnegative weight constraints can reduce risk from estimated covariances even when the true optimal portfolio contains shorts, giving a rigorous counterpoint to unrestricted plug-in mean--variance optimization and the 1/N benchmark. \ExtendedNote{exp-jagannathan-ma-constraints}{Shows why nonnegative weight constraints can reduce risk from estimated covariances even when the true optimal portfolio contains shorts, giving a rigorous counterpoint to unrestricted plug-in mean--variance optimization and the 1/N benchmark. Institutional readers should compare constrained, shrinkage, and equal-weight portfolios under the same investable universe and rebalance costs, rather than infer that a no-short rule is universally best. \ExtendedNote{exp-garleanu-pedersen-dynamic-costs}{Derives a costly-trading policy for several correlated assets and predictors with different decay rates: aim toward expected future targets and adjust only partway today. \section{Performance measurement, attribution and manager evaluation}\label{catalogue-section-6-performance}
Separate return calculation, attribution, risk adjustment and skill inference. Smoothed returns, survivorship and luck can make an ordinary record look exceptional.

\section{Asset--liability management}\label{catalogue-section-6-5}
\label{sec:depth-alm}
\ExtendedNote{subject-17}{Define the liability before optimizing the assets. For a defined-benefit plan, model promised nominal and inflation-linked benefits, contributions and sponsor support; for an insurer, contractual claims and capital; for an endowment, a spending policy; and for a sovereign pool, its fiscal withdrawal rule. Track both surplus value (assets less marked liabilities) and cash available on each payment or collateral date. Existing \hyperref[sec:gap-inflation]{inflation instruments}, \hyperref[sec:gap-private-equity]{private-fund cash flows}, and \hyperref[sec:gap-insurance-linked]{longevity-risk} readings supply components, not a complete ALM policy.}
\href{catalogue_extended_notes.html\#subject-17}{Subject context and qualifications}.
\CatalogueEntry{depth-alm-sharpe-tint-1990}{William F. Sharpe and Lawrence G. Tint, \href{https://doi.org/10.3905/jpm.1990.409248}{Liabilities---A New Approach}}{Advanced}{Research paper}{\emph{Journal of Portfolio Management} 16(2), 5--10, Winter 1990; version-of-record DOI, subscription access may apply.}{Places the liability in portfolio choice and asks what risk is measured relative to the obligation rather than only relative to cash. Define benefit cash flows and a liability valuation basis before estimating surplus covariance. Its early inflation-linked-security setting is not a modern pension rule or a full stochastic cash-flow model; benefits, contribution options and collateral needs need separate treatment.}{\href{catalogue_extended_notes.html\#depth-alm-sharpe-tint-1990}{Extended note}.}

\ExtendedNote{depth-alm-sharpe-tint-1990}{Places the liability in portfolio choice and asks what risk is measured relative to the obligation rather than only relative to cash. Read after mean--variance allocation and before duration hedging: the same bond can be risky in nominal asset space yet reduce surplus risk when it matches a promised payment. Define benefit cash flows and a liability valuation basis before estimating surplus covariance. Its early inflation-linked-security setting is not a modern pension rule or a full stochastic cash-flow model; benefits, contribution options and collateral needs need separate treatment.}
\CatalogueEntry{depth-alm-hoevenaars-2008}{Roy P. M. M. Hoevenaars, Roderick D. J. Molenaar, Peter C. Schotman and Tom B. M. Steenkamp, \href{https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jedc.2007.11.003}{Strategic Asset Allocation with Liabilities: Beyond Stocks and Bonds}}{Research}{Research paper}{\emph{Journal of Economic Dynamics and Control} 32(9), 2939--2970, September 2008; published article, author-university record.}{Models inflation and real-rate risk in pension liabilities and estimates intertemporal covariance among liabilities, bonds, equities and alternatives. It separates the global minimum-variance portfolio from a liability hedge, then shows why asset-only and surplus-optimal allocations differ. Read after Sharpe--Tint and the long-horizon allocation texts. Estimated VAR dynamics and pre-2008 market data are model and sample dependent; real-world liquidity, leverage and collateral may make a statistical hedge infeasible.}{\href{catalogue_extended_notes.html\#depth-alm-hoevenaars-2008}{Extended note}.}

\ExtendedNote{depth-alm-hoevenaars-2008}{Models inflation and real-rate risk in pension liabilities and estimates intertemporal covariance among liabilities, bonds, equities and alternatives. It separates the global minimum-variance portfolio from a liability hedge, then shows why asset-only and surplus-optimal allocations differ. \subsection{Rough and path-dependent volatility}\label{catalogue-section-7-1-sub-rough-and-path-dependent-volatility}
\CatalogueEntry{s6-rough}{Jim Gatheral, Thibault Jaisson and Mathieu Rosenbaum, \href{https://arxiv.org/abs/1410.3394}{``Volatility Is Rough''}}{Research}{Research paper}{2018}{First circulated as a 2014 preprint and published in 2018. Documents a fractional scaling structure in high-frequency volatility and introduces rough volatility as a parsimonious explanation. It changed the research agenda for volatility forecasting and option-surface dynamics, but implementation requires care over estimation noise and discretisation. \sourcecite{11}}{\textit{Applications:} Equity and index volatility, options. }

\CatalogueEntry{add-pdv}{Julien Guyon and Jordan Lekeufack, \href{https://doi.org/10.1080/14697688.2023.2221281}{Volatility Is (Mostly) Path-Dependent}}{Research}{Research paper}{Quantitative Finance 23(9), 1221--1258, 2023; published online 19 July 2023; DOI 10.1080/14697688.2023.2221281.}{Fits index implied and realised volatility using weighted histories of returns and squared returns, then builds a path-dependent continuous-time volatility model with exponential-kernel Markovian approximations. It gives a concrete alternative to interpreting every persistent volatility pattern as fractional roughness. Study the historical-versus-risk-neutral parameter distinction, train/test split and joint SPX/VIX smile fit before comparing it with rough Bergomi or rough Heston. Publisher abstract claims high explanatory power in its equity-index samples; it does not establish universal performance across assets, volatility regimes or tradable hedges after costs.}{\href{catalogue_extended_notes.html\#add-pdv}{Extended note}.}

\ExtendedNote{add-pdv}{The publisher's issue listing verifies the article, authors, pages and July 2023 online date; its abstract describes the return and squared-return kernels, the continuous-time PDV model and a four-factor Markovian approximation. The author-linked code repository is identified in publisher search text, but no code execution or full-text derivation check was performed. For a reproduction, fix the filtration, close-to-close convention, implied-versus-realised target, option quote filter and calibration loss before comparing models. Report pricing errors, stability, runtime and hedge outcomes separately; a good volatility regression need not make a sound risk-neutral pricing model.}
\CatalogueEntry{add-vol-comparison}{Eduardo Abi Jaber and Shaun (Xiaoyuan) Li, \href{https://doi.org/10.1111/mafi.12463}{Volatility Models in Practice: Rough, Path-Dependent, or Markovian?}}{Research}{Research paper}{Mathematical Finance 35(4), 796--817, October 2025; first published online 6 May 2025; DOI 10.1111/mafi.12463.}{Compares rough, path-dependent and Markovian models against SPX option smiles using matched parameter budgets. The publisher abstract reports that the tested rough specifications miss the global at-the-money skew shape and underperform a one-factor Markovian benchmark over one week to three months; a non-rough path-dependent and a two-factor Markovian model fit one-week to three-year smiles better in the study. Use it to design matched calibration and hedging comparisons after the PDV and rough-volatility foundations. These sample-specific option-price results do not prove that every rough model fails or that lower fit error yields better hedges.}{\href{catalogue_extended_notes.html\#add-vol-comparison}{Extended note}.}

\ExtendedNote{add-vol-comparison}{The publisher article page identifies two authors, journal location, online publication date and abstract. The paper's comparison is especially valuable because nominally richer rough dynamics can be tested against simpler Markovian alternatives with similar parameter counts. For a desk exercise, use identical SPX quote filters, bid--ask weights, maturities, calibration frequency and runtime hardware, then evaluate interpolation, out-of-sample smiles and hedge errors separately. The abstract's specific findings concern the examined models and SPX sample. Research data are listed as not shared; full text and an independent reproduction were not inspected here.}

\section{Surfaces, rough volatility and calibration}\label{catalogue-section-7-2}
\label{sec:exp-surface-numerics}
Read Gatheral and Bergomi first. Progress from static arbitrage and tail constraints to stochastic dynamics, efficient numerical pricing and learned calibration; each step answers a different validation question.
\Needspace{8\baselineskip}
\subsection{Surfaces and calibration}\label{catalogue-section-7-2-sub-surfaces-and-calibration}
\CatalogueEntry{exp-lee-wings}{Roger W. Lee, \href{https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.0960-1627.2004.00200.x}{The Moment Formula for Implied Volatility at Extreme Strikes}; \href{https://math.uchicago.edu/~rogerlee/moment.pdf}{author manuscript}}{Research}{Research paper}{Mathematical Finance 14(3), 469--480 (2004); first published 18 June 2004.}{Derives model-independent links between the asymptotic slope of total implied variance and finite positive or inverse moments of the underlying distribution. It gives a disciplined boundary check for wing extrapolation when listed strikes are sparse, and helps distinguish a surface that fits observed quotes from one with defensible tail behaviour. The formula constrains asymptotic slopes; it does not identify a unique extrapolated price or settle finite-strike liquidity and event-risk assumptions.}{}

\ExtendedNote{exp-gatheral-jacquier-svi}{Constructs a tractable SVI implied-volatility surface and calibration conditions that rule out static butterfly and calendar arbitrage. \section{Delta hedging, transaction costs and smile dynamics}\label{catalogue-section-7-hedging}
\label{sec:option-hedging}
An option model is finally judged by the hedge it implies. These readings show what happens to a delta hedge when volatility is misspecified, rebalancing is discrete and trading is costly, how to attribute option profit and loss to its Greeks, and which delta to use when the smile moves with the underlying. The practitioner texts by Natenberg and Taleb are in Section~\ref{catalogue-section-7-1}; learned and scenario-based hedges follow in Section~\ref{catalogue-section-7-3}.
\CatalogueEntry{vo-el-karoui-jeanblanc-shreve-1998}{Nicole El Karoui, Monique Jeanblanc-Picqué and Steven E. Shreve, \href{https://doi.org/10.1111/1467-9965.00047}{``Robustness of the Black and Scholes Formula''}}{Research}{Research paper}{Mathematical Finance, 8(2), 93--126 (1998); DOI 10.1111/1467-9965.00047.}{If a hedger's assumed volatility, a function of time and the stock price, dominates the true stochastic volatility, the resulting price dominates the true price and the hedge super-replicates almost surely; the reverse holds when it is dominated. The comparison can fail when the assumed volatility is not a function of time and price. The results cover European and American options and give a bound and hedge for Asian options.}{}

\section{Hedging with learning and scenarios}\label{catalogue-section-7-3}
\label{sec:exp-deep-hedging}
\ExtendedNote{subject-99}{Section~\ref{sec:s12-control} adds partial-information trading with GRU/DDPG, the corrected Bai et al. review and regime-switching equilibrium control. The main limitation in financial RL is not network capacity but environment credibility. A policy can only learn the fills, impact, counterparty behaviour and regime transitions encoded by its simulator; in market making, its own actions also alter the state distribution. Offline policy evaluation, conservative objectives, simple benchmark policies and simulator validation are therefore more important than marginal algorithmic novelty.}
\href{catalogue_extended_notes.html\#subject-99}{Subject context and qualifications}.
These readings connect learned market dynamics to specific hedge decisions. Compare with delta and delta-vega baselines, then examine the traded instruments, transaction costs and stress regimes behind any claimed improvement.

\Needspace{13\baselineskip}
\section{Variance, correlation, VIX and dividends}\label{catalogue-section-7-4}
\label{sec:gap-volatility-premia}
Separate the payoff being traded from the risk premium being estimated. Move from variance replication to index-versus-single-name correlation, volatility futures and dividend strips, using methodology documents and explicit counter-evidence to test implementation. Single-stock option returns, and short-dated and retail option trading, have their own subsections; option-implied densities and tail risk follow in Section~\ref{catalogue-section-7-implied}.
\Needspace{8\baselineskip}

\ExtendedNote{gap-correlation-risk}{Uses index and constituent options to investigate the pricing of correlation risk. It gives dispersion research an economic framework beyond comparing index implied volatility with a weighted average of single-name volatilities. Reconstruct index weights, strike exposure, maturity and rebalancing before attributing a spread to correlation. \ExtendedNote{gap-cboe-vix6}{The authoritative operational companion for VIX research: identifies the option inputs, maturity handling, calculation and dissemination conventions, and the distinction between the spot index and derivatives settlement. Reproduce a worked calculation and separately model the special opening quotation used at expiry. Historical backtests need the methodology applicable at the time, consistent option timestamps and missing-quote handling. An index value is a calculated benchmark; it is not the execution price of a variance swap, a futures contract or a volatility ETP.}

\ExtendedNote{gap-vix-premium}{Studies the premium in VIX futures relative to a statistical expectation of future VIX and links its behaviour to hedging demand and trader positions. Read it after variance risk premia to distinguish a futures premium, a realised-variance payoff and the convexity effects of volatility. Useful for term-structure and relative-value research, but forecasting uncertainty and position data are integral to the argument. A steep futures curve is not sufficient evidence of an exploitable premium or a stable rolling strategy.}

Read directly after van Binsbergen, Brandt and Koijen to compare the cash-flow construction and economic interpretation rather than treating the original result as settled. \section{Option-implied densities, recovery and tail risk}\label{catalogue-section-7-implied}
\label{sec:option-implied-information}
Option prices across strikes reveal the market's risk-neutral distribution. These readings extract it, extend it into the tails, try to separate beliefs from risk aversion, and test what it forecasts; jump and tail premia are measured from the same quotes. The Breeden--Litzenberger density result is in Section~\ref{catalogue-section-7-1}, the Bakshi--Kapadia--Madan moment estimators in Section~\ref{catalogue-section-7-4}, and Horvath's arbitrage-based recovery with model-free pricing in Section~\ref{catalogue-section-7-2}.

\section{Convertibles, exotics and structured products}\label{catalogue-section-7-5}
\label{sec:gap-hybrid-products}
\ExtendedNote{subject-55}{These instruments join optionality to credit, financing and contractual exercise rules. Read the convertible handbook before the default-aware model, and use the autocallable numerical paper with the earlier Monte Carlo, PDE and hedging foundations. The term sheet defines the state and stopping rules. Exotic payoffs need the barrier, static-hedging and model-risk readings; retail structured products add issuer margins and distribution incentives, which the evidence papers measure against model values.}
\href{catalogue_extended_notes.html\#subject-55}{Subject context and qualifications}.

\ExtendedNote{gap-convertible-handbook}{Introduces a hybrid market where equity optionality, issuer credit, contractual calls and puts, dividends and stock borrow interact. Use it to build a term-sheet checklist and an attribution separating equity delta, volatility, credit spread, rates and financing. Convertible arbitrage cannot be understood as a simple option plus a risk-free bond: default treatment and changing borrow availability matter. Historical market examples require current confirmations, corporate-action adjustments and financing inputs before they can inform live relative value.}

\ExtendedNote{gap-convertible-credit}{Develops convertible valuation with explicit treatment of credit events and the associated stock-price behaviour. It is a technical companion to the handbook for examining how default, recovery and contractual exercise features enter a numerical pricing problem. Compare alternative assumptions before interpreting a calibrated credit spread as a structural parameter. Callable and puttable features require careful exercise logic and numerical convergence; apparently similar bond/equity decompositions can produce inconsistent values when their default assumptions differ.}

\subsection{Fractional shares, odd lots and contract size}\label{catalogue-section-8-1-sub-fractional-shares-odd-lots-and-contract-size}
\label{sec:fractional-shares}
Trading in units smaller than a round lot or a whole share: fractional trading at retail brokers and how it is reported, odd lots in the consolidated data, the nominal share price, and smaller option and futures contracts. Tokenised fractional claims are in \hyperref[catalogue-section-18-tokenised-assets]{Tokenised securities and real-world assets}.
\CatalogueEntry{ft-bartlett-mccrary-ohara-2024}{Robert P. Bartlett, Justin McCrary and Maureen O'Hara, \href{https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jfineco.2024.103836}{``Tiny trades, big questions: Fractional shares''}}{Research}{Research paper}{Journal of Financial Economics, 157, 103836 (2024); DOI 10.1016/j.jfineco.2024.103836.}{Identifies fractional-share trades on the consolidated tape by the execution latency of the two largest fractional broker-dealers (Robinhood and DriveWealth). High-priced stocks, meme stocks, IPOs, SPACs and popular retail names have many tiny trades, largely the fractional legs of dollar-based orders; the measure predicts liquidity and volatility and proxies app-based retail trading. Reporting rules then rounded fractions up, inflating volume and censoring samples.}{}

\section{Queues, placement and market making}\label{catalogue-section-8-3}
\label{sec:exp-execution}
Use Harris, Hasbrouck, Cartea and Almgren--Chriss as foundations. The papers below move from queue dynamics and routing to inventory control and dealer markets, with explicit assumptions about fills and participant response.
\Needspace{8\baselineskip}
\subsection{Queues, placement and point processes}\label{catalogue-section-8-3-sub-queues-placement-and-point-processes}
\CatalogueEntry{exp-cont-delarrard-markov-lob}{Rama Cont; Adrien de Larrard, \href{https://epubs.siam.org/doi/10.1137/110856605}{Price Dynamics in a Markovian Limit Order Market}; \href{https://arxiv.org/abs/1104.4596}{author preprint}}{Research}{Research paper}{SIAM Journal on Financial Mathematics 4(1), 1--25 (2013); online 29 January 2013.}{Models limit and market orders plus cancellations as a queueing system so price changes emerge when book queues deplete. It is a useful theoretical baseline before queue-reactive simulators, passive fill models or learned execution policies. The small Markovian state omits long-memory order flow, venue latency, hidden liquidity and strategic responses to one's own orders, so it is not sufficient as a production fill simulator.}{\href{catalogue_extended_notes.html\#exp-cont-delarrard-markov-lob}{Extended note}.}

\ExtendedNote{exp-cont-delarrard-markov-lob}{Models limit and market orders plus cancellations as a queueing system so price changes emerge when book queues deplete. The analytical waiting-time, direction and diffusion-limit results turn order-book imbalance from an opaque feature into a state variable with explicit assumptions. It is a useful theoretical baseline before queue-reactive simulators, passive fill models or learned execution policies. The small Markovian state omits long-memory order flow, venue latency, hidden liquidity and strategic responses to one's own orders, so it is not sufficient as a production fill simulator.}

\ExtendedNote{exp-huang-lehalle-rosenbaum-queue-reactive}{Estimates state-dependent order-arrival and cancellation intensities during intervals with a fixed reference price, then stitches those intervals into a full book simulator. \ExtendedNote{exp-cont-kukanov-order-placement}{Formulates the immediate choice of limit versus market orders and allocation across fragmented exchanges as a convex order-placement problem. \ExtendedNote{exp-bergault-gueant-otc-multiasset}{Extends inventory-aware OTC quoting to many correlated assets and different RFQ trade sizes, then uses a factor representation to reduce the numerical dimension. \section{Simulation and counterfactual validation}\label{catalogue-section-8-5}
\label{sec:exp-simulation}
Read after the queueing and impact models, alongside ABIDES and JAX-LOB. Matching unconditional price statistics, reproducing order events and predicting responses to an intervention are distinct levels of evidence.
\CatalogueEntry{exp-vadori-otc-marl}{Nelson Vadori et al., \href{https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/mafi.12416}{Towards multi-agent reinforcement learning-driven over-the-counter market simulations}}{Research}{Research paper}{Mathematical Finance 34(2), 262--347 (2024); first published online 20 September 2023.}{Models a dealer OTC market as interacting liquidity providers and takers whose policies learn quoting, hedging, execution and market-share trade-offs. Shared-policy learning and a calibration procedure make it an institutional complement to exchange-book simulators such as ABIDES and JAX-LOB, especially for FX-style bilateral flow. Before using it for policy selection, benchmark against observed RFQ flow, tiering, rejection rates, hedging venues and regime-specific client response.}{\href{catalogue_extended_notes.html\#exp-vadori-otc-marl}{Extended note}.}
\EntryRecency{exp-vadori-otc-marl}{Inherited publication/version chronology (date roles retained): Mathematical Finance 34(2), 262–347 (2024); first published online 20 September 2023.}{Mathematical Finance 34(2), 262--347 (2024); first published online 20 September 2023.}{2026-10-04 (inherited metadata evidence; not a fresh source check in this expansion)}{Inherited metadata screen for selected linked sources. It does not verify every source in a paired entry, full text, legal currency or empirical results. \href{archive/depth-recency-2026-10-04/catalogue-recency-url-ledger.json}{URL-level scope ledger}.}{No superseding source established by this expansion; this is not a finding that none exists.}{Annual publication/correction check; quarterly for a living report or recent frontier result.}
\ExtendedNote{exp-vadori-otc-marl}{Models a dealer OTC market as interacting liquidity providers and takers whose policies learn quoting, hedging, execution and market-share trade-offs. Shared-policy learning and a calibration procedure make it an institutional complement to exchange-book simulators such as ABIDES and JAX-LOB, especially for FX-style bilateral flow. The paper studies emergent skewing and hedging inside a simulated game; those behaviours depend on reward design and opponent populations. Before using it for policy selection, benchmark against observed RFQ flow, tiering, rejection rates, hedging venues and regime-specific client response.}

\ExtendedNote{exp-nagy-lob-bench}{Provides a reproducible evaluation suite for generated LOBSTER-format message-by-order data, testing conditional and unconditional spreads, volumes, imbalance, inter-arrival times, discriminator scores and event-specific price responses. \ExtendedNote{exp-li-mars-simulator}{Introduces an order-level generative market model and interactive simulator intended to respond to participant actions while allowing controlled market scenarios. \ExtendedNote{exp-kang-relobgen-replayability}{Makes generated LOB messages executable against the current resting book by choosing eligible referenced orders and masking invalid event fields, avoiding post-hoc correction or rejection. This addresses a concrete failure mode in closed-loop generative simulators: a cancellation or execution that refers to an absent order cannot produce a valid fill path. The paper reports full replayability over 500-message rollouts and a speed advantage over LOBS5; that narrow test does not validate longer feedback loops, market impact, queue priority or strategy outcomes across venues. Read as an implementation check on MarS-like generators.}

\section{Dealer market making in bonds, swaps and FX}\label{catalogue-section-8-dealer}
\label{sec:dealer-market-making}
Bond, swap and currency dealers quote on request or stream prices to clients, then decide whether to hold the resulting inventory, offset it against later client flow or hedge it with other dealers. These readings cover dealer quoting models, evidence on dealer inventory, balance-sheet capacity and networks, and FX practices such as internalisation, aggregators and last look. The previous section covers the same markets from the client's side.
\Needspace{8\baselineskip}

\section{Options, futures and ETF execution}\label{catalogue-section-8-asset-class}
Execution differs by instrument: option dealers hedge discretely and price volatility risk, futures trade under exchange matching and settlement rules, and ETFs and index funds concentrate trading around creations, reconstitutions and the close.

\chapter{Funding, collateral and securities lending}\label{catalogue-chapter-9}
Funding, collateral and borrow connect valuation with feasible positions. Securities lending has its own supply, recall, fee and settlement mechanisms. CFDs and total return swaps deliver the same exposure synthetically, priced by their financing, borrow and margin terms.
\Needspace{13\baselineskip}
\section{Funding liquidity, demand and crowded trades}\label{catalogue-section-9-1}
\label{sec:exp-funding-crowding}
These readings explain how positions, intermediary capacity and common demand can change prices and the cost of exiting. Connect them to risk budgeting and transaction-cost research before interpreting a factor return as scalable alpha.
\Needspace{8\baselineskip}

\CatalogueEntry{exp-kruttli-ltcm-redux}{Mathias S. Kruttli, Phillip J. Monin, Lubomir Petrasek, and Sumudu W. Watugala, \href{https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0304405X2500025X}{LTCM Redux? Hedge Fund Treasury Trading, Funding Fragility, and Risk Constraints}; \href{https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/phillip-monin.htm}{Federal Reserve author publication record}}{Research}{Research paper}{Journal of Financial Economics 169, article 104017, July 2025; DOI 10.1016/j.jfineco.2025.104017.}{Uses granular regulatory fund and creditor data around March 2020 to show Treasury arbitrageurs cut positions and held more cash while average repo financing remained broadly stable; internal VaR constraints and precautionary liquidity were more explanatory than a simple repo-credit shutoff. Evidence is episode- and filing-specific, so institutional scenario design should stress both external financing and internally imposed limits, client concentration, margin calls, and same-day liquidity needs.}{\href{catalogue_extended_notes.html\#exp-kruttli-ltcm-redux}{Extended note}.}
\EntryRecency{exp-kruttli-ltcm-redux}{July 2025}{Journal of Financial Economics 169, 104017; DOI 10.1016/j.jfineco.2025.104017}{2026-10-04}{\href{https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0304405X2500025X}{Elsevier journal record} confirms article number, volume, date, DOI and abstract; \href{https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/phillip-monin.htm}{Federal Reserve coauthor bibliography} confirms all four authors and journal publication.}{Selected 2025 journal version follows an earlier Fed/SSRN working paper; no content equivalence assumed.}{Annual publication/link check; revisit new Treasury-market evidence before generalising the March 2020 results.}
\ExtendedNote{exp-kruttli-ltcm-redux}{Uses granular regulatory fund and creditor data around March 2020 to show Treasury arbitrageurs cut positions and held more cash while average repo financing remained broadly stable; internal VaR constraints and precautionary liquidity were more explanatory than a simple repo-credit shutoff. This directly sharpens the funding-liquidity spiral foundation and prevents every Treasury unwind from being labelled a haircut shock. Evidence is episode- and filing-specific, so institutional scenario design should stress both external financing and internally imposed limits, client concentration, margin calls, and same-day liquidity needs.}

\ExtendedNote{exp-monin-treasury-decomposition}{Decomposes large hedge funds' September 2025 Treasury longs into estimated cash--futures basis, swap-spread, maturity-matched, curve, and liquidity uses, rather than treating all cash bonds or all short futures as basis trades. \section{CFDs, total return swaps and synthetic exposure}\label{catalogue-section-9-synthetic}
\label{sec:cfd-synthetic}
A contract for difference or equity total return swap delivers the price change of a share or index without ownership. Its cost sits in the financing spread, dividend and borrow pass-through, and margin and counterparty terms. The same contract raises disclosure and tax questions for institutions, and leverage and conduct questions when sold to retail clients.

\part{Markets and instruments}
\chapter{Equities}\label{catalogue-chapter-10}
Combine cash-flow valuation, factor evidence, short-selling and other trader signals, corporate events, statistical arbitrage and market structure, then combine the signals into long--short portfolios. Research validation and cost-aware portfolio methods are cross-cutting prerequisites.

\CatalogueEntry{add-index-effect}{Robin Greenwood and Marco Sammon, \href{https://dash.harvard.edu/entities/publication/2cc676bd-c8da-40e7-b112-3ecc8644e687}{The Disappearing Index Effect}}{Research}{Research paper}{The Journal of Finance 80(2), 657--698, April 2025; DOI 10.1111/jofi.13410; Harvard open manuscript record.}{Re-examines the price response to S\&P 500 additions and deletions as passive ownership grew. \ExtendedNote{add-index-effect}{The Harvard publication record provides authors, April 2025 Journal of Finance identity, DOI, open manuscript and abstract. Read alongside earnings events and ETF creation/redemption mechanics: index inclusion can affect ownership and demand, but announcement timing, pre-positioning and arbitrage capital change the price path. Define the index family, addition/deletion sample and abnormal-return model before comparing decades. Test the announcement-to-effective window separately from post-effective reversal, and budget auction and close-price execution costs. The linked manuscript was available but the review relied on the institutional record and abstract rather than a new full-paper replication.}

\section{Valuation and ETFs}\label{catalogue-section-10-2}
\label{sec:gap-equity-etf}
Cash-flow valuation complements the factor and event-driven readings. ETFs add a vehicle layer whose creation, redemption and price-discovery mechanisms vary with the underlying market; read the contrasting equity and bond evidence together.

\subsection{ETFs, indexing and passive ownership}\label{catalogue-section-10-2-sub-etfs-indexing-and-passive-ownership}
\CatalogueEntry{gap-madhavan-etf}{Ananth N. Madhavan, \href{https://academic.oup.com/book/3366}{Exchange-Traded Funds and the New Dynamics of Investing}}{Advanced}{Book / monograph}{Oxford University Press, published 1 August 2016; print ISBN 9780190279394.}{A coherent entry to ETF economics, index investing, factor exposures and the links between funds and their underlying markets. Use it before studying ETF premiums, creation and redemption, execution quality, and the choice between a fund and direct securities. ETF shares, underlying holdings and published NAVs can have different liquidity and valuation times, so a displayed premium is not automatically an arbitrage opportunity.}{\href{catalogue_extended_notes.html\#gap-madhavan-etf}{Extended note}.}
\EntryRecency{gap-madhavan-etf}{Published 1 August 2016}{Oxford book DOI 10.1093/acprof:oso/9780190279394.001.0001; print ISBN 9780190279394}{2026-10-04}{\href{https://academic.oup.com/book/3366}{Oxford Academic book record} confirms Ananth N. \ExtendedNote{gap-madhavan-etf}{A coherent entry to ETF economics, index investing, factor exposures and the links between funds and their underlying markets. Use it before studying ETF premiums, creation and redemption, execution quality, and the choice between a fund and direct securities. The author's industry perspective is useful but should be paired with independent empirical evidence. ETF shares, underlying holdings and published NAVs can have different liquidity and valuation times, so a displayed premium is not automatically an arbitrage opportunity.}
\CatalogueEntry{gap-etf-volatility}{Itzhak Ben-David, Francesco Franzoni and Rabih Moussawi, \href{https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/jofi.12727}{Do ETFs Increase Volatility?}}{Research}{Research paper}{Journal of Finance 73(6), 2471--2535, December 2018 issue; first published online 22 September 2018.}{Studies how ETF ownership can transmit trading shocks to constituent equities through the arbitrage mechanism. Read alongside ETF mechanics to distinguish price discovery, temporary price pressure and changes in fundamental risk. The empirical design and equity-market setting matter: ownership is endogenous, measured volatility depends on horizon, and the result should not be transferred mechanically to bond ETFs or interpreted as proof that every passive flow destabilises prices.}{\href{catalogue_extended_notes.html\#gap-etf-volatility}{Extended note}.}
\EntryRecency{gap-etf-volatility}{First published online 22 September 2018; December 2018 issue}{The Journal of Finance 73(6), 2471--2535; DOI 10.1111/jofi.12727}{2026-10-04}{\href{https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/jofi.12727}{Wiley journal record} confirms all three authors, online date, December issue, pages and the earlier working title ``ETFs, Arbitrage, and Shock Propagation.}{The journal article supersedes its earlier working-title manuscript; the title change should not create a duplicate catalogue record.}{Annual article/supporting-information link check; treat market result as sample-specific.}
\ExtendedNote{gap-etf-volatility}{Studies how ETF ownership can transmit trading shocks to constituent equities through the arbitrage mechanism. Read alongside ETF mechanics to distinguish price discovery, temporary price pressure and changes in fundamental risk. Useful for event studies around index inclusion, fund flows and portfolio rebalancing. The empirical design and equity-market setting matter: ownership is endogenous, measured volatility depends on horizon, and the result should not be transferred mechanically to bond ETFs or interpreted as proof that every passive flow destabilises prices.}
\CatalogueEntry{gap-bond-etf-volatility}{Anna Agapova, Margarita Kaprielyan and Nikanor Volkov, \href{https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/fire.12426}{ETFs and the price volatility of underlying bonds}}{Research}{Research paper}{Financial Review 60(3), 667--700, 2025; online 16 January 2025.}{Examines corporate-bond ETF ownership and flows using 2010--2022 observations and finds an association between ownership and lower underlying bond volatility. Use the comparison to formulate competing liquidity-buffer and price-pressure hypotheses. The estimates are conditional on the sample and identification choices; they do not establish that all ETF structures remain stabilising in an unprecedented redemption shock.}{\href{catalogue_extended_notes.html\#gap-bond-etf-volatility}{Extended note}.}
\EntryRecency{gap-bond-etf-volatility}{Inherited publication/version chronology (date roles retained): Financial Review 60(3), 667–700, 2025; online 16 January 2025.}{Financial Review 60(3), 667--700, 2025; online 16 January 2025.}{2026-10-04 (inherited metadata evidence; not a fresh source check in this expansion)}{Inherited metadata screen for selected linked sources. \ExtendedNote{gap-bond-etf-volatility}{Examines corporate-bond ETF ownership and flows using 2010--2022 observations and finds an association between ownership and lower underlying bond volatility. It is a useful contrast to equity ETF transmission studies and motivates separate treatment of investment-grade and high-yield bonds, flow direction and measurement horizon. Use the comparison to formulate competing liquidity-buffer and price-pressure hypotheses. The estimates are conditional on the sample and identification choices; they do not establish that all ETF structures remain stabilising in an unprecedented redemption shock.}

\section{Short selling and informed-trader signals}\label{catalogue-section-10-shorting}
\label{sec:equity-trader-signals}
Short sellers, option traders, insiders and retail investors leave records that can be used as stock signals: short interest and loan fees, option volume and implied-volatility spreads, insider filings and retail order flow. These readings separate information from short-sale constraints, borrow costs and attention, and record the rules that govern short-sale data. Section~\ref{catalogue-section-9-3} covers securities-lending mechanics and fees.
\Needspace{8\baselineskip}

\Needspace{13\baselineskip}
\section{Corporate events and merger arbitrage}\label{catalogue-section-10-events}
\label{sec:equity-events}
Event studies measure how prices respond to earnings announcements, analyst recommendations, equity issuance and takeover bids, and how much of the response is delayed. Long-horizon results depend heavily on method, so the methods readings come first. Merger arbitrage and other equity relative-value trades depend on deal completion, short-sale constraints and the supply of arbitrage capital.

\section{Signal combination and long--short portfolio construction}\label{catalogue-section-10-construction}
\label{sec:equity-construction}
These readings turn equity signals into a portfolio: scaling scores into return forecasts, combining many signals, aligning the alpha with the risk model and constraints, choosing sector neutrality and the size of the short side, and netting out trading costs. Section~\ref{catalogue-section-6-1} covers general portfolio theory, covariance estimation and factor risk models.

\chapter{Rates, inflation and cash instruments}\label{catalogue-chapter-11}

\CatalogueEntry{exp-gourinchas-ray-vayanos-preferred-habitat}{Pierre-Olivier Gourinchas, Walker Ray, and Dimitri Vayanos, \href{https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/aer.20220379}{A Preferred-Habitat Model of Term Premia, Exchange Rates, and Monetary Policy Spillovers}}{Research}{Research paper}{American Economic Review 115(11), 3788--3824, November 2025; DOI 10.1257/aer.20220379.}{Links currency and bond risk premia in a two-country preferred-habitat model with segmented investor clienteles and capital-constrained arbitrageurs. \EntryRecency{exp-gourinchas-ray-vayanos-preferred-habitat}{Inherited publication/version chronology (date roles retained): American Economic Review 115(11), 3788–3824, November 2025; DOI 10.1257/aer.20220379.}{American Economic Review 115(11), 3788--3824, November 2025; DOI 10.1257/aer.20220379.}{Not independently established at entry level in this expansion.}{Citation and annotation preserved from the pre-expansion catalogue. \href{bibliographic_audit.md}{Prior audit history} records bounded checks; no blanket fresh verification is inferred.}{No superseding source established by this expansion; this is not a finding that none exists.}{Annual publication/correction check; quarterly for a living report or recent frontier result.}
\ExtendedNote{exp-gourinchas-ray-vayanos-preferred-habitat}{Links currency and bond risk premia in a two-country preferred-habitat model with segmented investor clienteles and capital-constrained arbitrageurs. It gives a coherent mechanism for cross-border bond-purchase and policy spillovers, complementing the yield-curve, UIP, and FX-factor readings without treating every forward discount as an independent signal. An institution can use it to organize duration, FX hedge, and cross-border demand scenarios, but the equilibrium calibration does not supply a directly tradeable timing rule and requires market-specific flows and funding assumptions.}

Crump, and Emanuel Moench, \href{https://www.newyorkfed.org/research/staff\_reports/sr340.html}{Pricing the Term Structure with Linear Regressions}; \href{https://www.newyorkfed.org/research/data\_indicators/term-premia-tabs}{New York Fed ACM term-premium data notes}}{Research}{Research paper}{Journal of Financial Economics 110(1), 110--138, October 2013; New York Fed Staff Report 340 issued August 2008, revised April 2013.}{Estimates a no-arbitrage yield-curve model through a computationally convenient three-step linear-regression method, separating fitted expected short-rate and term-premium components. The premium is latent and depends on factor choice, historical sample, zero-coupon curve inputs, and revisions; a daily estimate should not be mistaken for a directly observed or guaranteed future bond return.}{\href{catalogue_extended_notes.html\#exp-adrian-crump-moench-term-structure}{Extended note}.}
\EntryRecency{exp-adrian-crump-moench-term-structure}{Staff Report August 2008, revised April 2013; journal October 2013}{Journal of Financial Economics 110(1), 110--138; DOI 10.1016/j.jfineco.2013.04.009}{2026-10-04}{\href{https://www.newyorkfed.org/research/staff_reports/sr340.html}{New York Fed report page} names Adrian, Crump and Moench, dates the report and explicitly identifies the published journal version; \href{https://www.newyorkfed.org/research/economists/crump/pub}{coauthor publication list} independently repeats the chronology.}{The journal article is the published successor to Staff Report 340; the Fed report remains the accessible selected reading.}{Annual article/data-note check; cite the journal when referring to the published result and check live ACM data notes separately.}
\ExtendedNote{exp-adrian-crump-moench-term-structure}{Estimates a no-arbitrage yield-curve model through a computationally convenient three-step linear-regression method, separating fitted expected short-rate and term-premium components. It turns the Fama--Bliss and Campbell--Shiller yield-curve questions into a reproducible estimation exercise and gives a common reference for interpreting published ACM term-premium series. The premium is latent and depends on factor choice, historical sample, zero-coupon curve inputs, and revisions; a daily estimate should not be mistaken for a directly observed or guaranteed future bond return.}

\ExtendedNote{exp-chaboud-off-run-treasury-liquidity}{Measures trading activity and liquidity in seasoned Treasuries, which are most of outstanding supply but differ materially from the on-the-run benchmark during stress. It fills a practical gap beside the BrokerTec on-the-run microstructure paper: issue age, CUSIP depth, dealer intermediation, and the ability to sell a specific cash bond matter for curve and basis portfolios. Some underlying regulatory transaction data are restricted, and market-structure proposals are prospective; cost and liquidation assumptions still need contemporaneous instrument-level validation.}

\section{Monetary policy, asset purchases and the yield curve}\label{catalogue-section-11-policy}
\label{sec:rates-policy-curve}
Policy expectations, term premia and central-bank balance sheets move the curve together. Measure surprises in narrow windows, adjust futures-implied paths for risk premia, and treat purchase or runoff effects as conditional on market functioning and on which securities change hands.
\CatalogueEntry{rt-kuttner-2001}{Kenneth N. Bill, note and bond yields barely respond to anticipated changes but respond strongly to surprises. The original futures-based policy-shock measure behind later event studies.}{}

\section{Government debt issuance, auctions and demand}\label{catalogue-section-11-issuance}
\label{sec:rates-issuance-demand}
Auction design, the issuance calendar, maturity choice and investor demand set the supply side of government debt. Read the dated Treasury documents with the auction and demand evidence; announcement and auction effects depend on dealer capacity and the holder base.

\section{Inflation and real yields}\label{catalogue-section-11-3}
\label{sec:gap-inflation}
Start with linker cash flows and index conventions, then the joint nominal/real pricing model, then breakeven decomposition and empirical evidence. Inflation expectations, inflation risk premia, liquidity and index basis are separate exposures.

\CatalogueEntry{gapclose-treasury-curve-data}{U.S. Department of the Treasury, \href{https://home.treasury.gov/policy-issues/financing-the-government/interest-rate-statistics/}{Interest Rate Statistics} and \href{https://home.treasury.gov/treasury-daily-interest-rate-xml-feed}{Daily Interest Rate XML Feed}}{Advanced}{Data / specification}{Living nominal and TIPS par-yield data and XML interface; methodology and availability inspected 4 October 2026.}{Treasury publishes daily nominal and real constant-maturity par-yield series with a documented XML query path. \EntryRecency{gapclose-treasury-curve-data}{Living official data series; TIPS real curve begins 2003}{Current XML feed and published methodology as inspected 4 October 2026}{2026-10-04}{Official Treasury \href{https://home.treasury.gov/policy-issues/financing-the-government/interest-rate-statistics/}{statistics/methodology page} and \href{https://home.treasury.gov/treasury-daily-interest-rate-xml-feed}{XML feed specification} inspected; no security-level quote tape obtained.}{Methodology breaks on 1 December 2008 for TIPS knot selection and 6 December 2021 for Treasury spline derivation; preserve historical official rates.}{Quarterly for feed or methodology changes; pin observation date and curve regime.}
\ExtendedNote{gapclose-treasury-curve-data}{The official XML feed allows a dated, reproducible comparison of published nominal and real constant-maturity par yields. Use it to check curve shape and breakeven arithmetic, retaining the data date and methodology era. It cannot independently reprice a selected CUSIP or establish a tradable hedge: the underlying indicative bid quotes are not supplied as security-level executable observations in this feed. Pair with Treasury auction results for a true awarded price on a specific issue, and source matched secondary-market prices separately for cross-sectional or forward-return tests.}

\ExtendedNote{gapclose-treasury-auction-data}{Use a named CUSIP and auction date to reproduce an actual awarded price and yield, then apply the issue terms and TIPS index ratio to a settlement cash-flow exercise. \Needspace{13\baselineskip}
\section{Sovereign and municipal debt}\label{catalogue-section-11-4}
\label{sec:gap-sovereign-municipal}
Distinguish local-currency from hard-currency claims, domestic from foreign law, and sovereign from subsovereign obligations. Debt sustainability and recovery processes provide economic scenarios; security-level disclosure, tax treatment and liquidity determine the actual investment.
\Needspace{8\baselineskip}
\subsection{Sovereign default, restructuring and local-currency debt}\label{catalogue-section-11-4-sub-sovereign-default-restructuring-and-local-currency-debt}
\CatalogueEntry{gap-sovereign-local-currency}{Wenxin Du and Jesse Schreger, \href{https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/jofi.12389}{Local Currency Sovereign Risk}}{Research}{Research paper}{The Journal of Finance 71(3), 1027--1070, June 2016; online 3 February 2016; DOI 10.1111/jofi.12389}{Constructs a local-currency sovereign credit spread against a synthetic local risk-free rate from cross-currency swaps, then compares its level and global-risk sensitivity with foreign-currency sovereign spreads. It is essential for separating currency and default exposures when comparing domestic bonds with hard-currency Eurobonds. Hedge availability, collateral, and law of issuance must be checked for each country and tenor.}{\href{catalogue_extended_notes.html\#gap-sovereign-local-currency}{Extended note}.}

\ExtendedNote{gap-sovereign-local-currency}{Constructs a local-currency sovereign credit spread against a synthetic local risk-free rate from cross-currency swaps, then compares its level and global-risk sensitivity with foreign-currency sovereign spreads. It is essential for separating currency and default exposures when comparing domestic bonds with hard-currency Eurobonds. The wedge can also reflect capital controls, selective default, and market frictions, so the swap benchmark is not a pure counterfactual in stressed markets. Hedge availability, collateral, and law of issuance must be checked for each country and tenor.}

\ExtendedNote{gap-sovereign-haircuts}{Builds a historical investor-loss database for 180 sovereign restructurings in 68 countries and connects larger present-value haircuts with higher subsequent spreads and longer market exclusion. It supplies recovery and reputation evidence absent from a standard sovereign yield decomposition. A sovereign-credit desk should model the value and timing of exchanged instruments, not equate a face-value reduction with economic loss. The sample ends in 2010, and associations do not imply an invariant causal penalty; legal terms, official-sector treatment, and creditor mix vary across later episodes.}

\ExtendedNote{gap-sovereign-imf-srdsf}{Sets out the IMF framework for near-term sovereign stress signals, debt fan charts, gross financing needs, and judgment in market-access country analysis. It gives a consistent way to connect a sovereign bond's maturity ladder and currency mix to fiscal and refinancing scenarios, rather than reading a spread in isolation. The framework is designed for surveillance and program analysis, not security pricing or trading signals. \section{Cash and money markets}\label{catalogue-section-11-5}
\label{sec:gap-money-markets}
Short maturity does not remove rollover, liquidity or counterparty risk. Combine funding-market economics with fund holdings and instrument definitions; use the earlier repo and securities-lending readings for secured financing and collateral specialness.
\CatalogueEntry{gap-money-cp-cd-primer}{Matteo Aquilina, Andreas Schrimpf and Karamfil Todorov, \href{https://www.bis.org/publications/qr-202309/cp-and-cds-markets-primer}{CP and CDs Markets: A Primer}}{Advanced}{Research paper}{BIS Quarterly Review special feature, published 18 September 2023.}{Explains issuance and investor structure of commercial paper and negotiable certificates of deposit across major currencies, and documents the reduced but still important role of money-market funds in absorbing short-term paper. It clarifies that CP and CDs rarely trade before maturity, so liquidity analysis cannot assume continuous bond-market price discovery. The cross-jurisdictional aggregates are historical and imperfect; issuer credit, programme support, and live placement capacity require instrument-level evidence.}{\href{catalogue_extended_notes.html\#gap-money-cp-cd-primer}{Extended note}.}
\EntryRecency{gap-money-cp-cd-primer}{Published 18 September 2023}{BIS Quarterly Review special feature by Matteo Aquilina, Andreas Schrimpf and Karamfil Todorov}{2026-10-04}{\href{https://www.bis.org/publications/qr-202309/cp-and-cds-markets-primer}{BIS full-text feature} and \href{https://www.bis.org/publications/qr-202309}{BIS issue page} confirm author identity, date and institutional series.}{This is an institutional feature, not a journal article; no later edition claim.}{Annual link and BIS data-update check; date market-size statements to the article period.}
\ExtendedNote{gap-money-cp-cd-primer}{Explains issuance and investor structure of commercial paper and negotiable certificates of deposit across major currencies, and documents the reduced but still important role of money-market funds in absorbing short-term paper. It clarifies that CP and CDs rarely trade before maturity, so liquidity analysis cannot assume continuous bond-market price discovery. Use it to map issuer rollover, investor concentration, currency, and maturity ladder for cash portfolios. The cross-jurisdictional aggregates are historical and imperfect; issuer credit, programme support, and live placement capacity require instrument-level evidence.}

\chapter{Credit and securitisation}\label{catalogue-chapter-12}
Distinguish issuer and collateral cash flows, recourse, recovery, tranching and optionality. Legal and reporting resources complement pricing models and empirical evidence.
