\CatalogueEntry{add-cds-model}{ISDA and S\&P Global, \href{https://www.cdsmodel.com/download.html}{ISDA CDS Standard Model, source code and test grids}}{Advanced}{Data / specification}{Production version 1.8.3, released and effective 7 April 2021; official download and documentation pages checked 4 October 2026.}{Supplies the standard single-name CDS valuation implementation and published IBOR/RFR test grids. Use it after O'Kane to reconcile trade dates, accrual, recovery, discount factors, hazard calibration and the conversion between quoted running spread and upfront fee. Reproduce a documented example and compare an independent implementation at multiple maturities and recovery assumptions. The production code version is 2021, while curve inputs and contractual documents have separate revision histories. A matching model output does not prove that a trade confirmation, settlement price or observed bond-CDS basis is correct.}{\href{catalogue_extended_notes.html\#add-cds-model}{Extended note}.}
\EntryRecency{add-cds-model}{7 April 2021}{Production 1.8.3}{2026-10-04}{Official download page lists production version, effective/release date, RFR validation change and IBOR qualification.; Official documentation page exposes specification and test-grid links; source-code/test-grid execution was not performed. \href{https://www.cdsmodel.com/download.html}{Primary source inspected}.}{Earlier production versions 1.8–1.8.2 for the site's current production download.}{Quarterly}
\ExtendedNote{add-cds-model}{Treat the model, rate-curve specification and trade documentation as distinct inputs with their own dates. Reproduce a standard running-spread/upfront conversion using the official test grids, then vary recovery, step-in and cash-settlement dates, coupon and discount curve. Check conventions for clean versus dirty upfront and accrued premium before comparing to a dealer screen. Version 1.8.3 changes validation to permit swap-only RFR curves and supports IBOR as well as RFR rates; the official page says it does not change IBOR calculations. The public implementation is a calculation reference, not a trade-specific confirmation or independently verified market quote.}

Reprice an otherwise unchanged CDS under the chosen RFR curve and a historical IBOR setup to isolate rate-input effects from spread, recovery and contract changes. \section{Covered bonds}\label{catalogue-section-12-3}
\label{sec:depth-covered-bonds}
\ExtendedNote{subject-30}{Begin with the statutory claim, then model the issuer and the dynamic cover pool jointly. A covered bond is an issuer liability with a preferential claim on segregated assets; its spread is therefore neither a simple senior-bank spread nor a securitisation-tranche spread. Compare contractual and national-law terms before using cross-market prices.}
\href{catalogue_extended_notes.html\#subject-30}{Subject context and qualifications}.
\CatalogueEntry{depth-covered-eu-directive}{European Union, \href{https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2019/2162/oj/eng}{Directive (EU) 2019/2162 on covered bonds}}{Not specified}{Contract / specification / guidance}{Official Journal text, 2019; read Articles 4--6 and 10--17 alongside applicable national implementing law}{Defines dual recourse, bankruptcy remoteness, eligible cover assets, segregation, coverage and liquidity buffers. Article 17 confines extendable maturity to objective triggers and specifies its effect on claims and priority. Prerequisite: distinguish the issuer's unsecured estate from the cover-pool estate and map asset collections, overcollateralisation and extension dates. The Directive establishes an EU framework, not identical national collateral eligibility, supervisory practice or a quoted fair spread.}{\href{catalogue_extended_notes.html\#depth-covered-eu-directive}{Extended note}.}

\ExtendedNote{depth-covered-eu-directive}{Defines dual recourse, bankruptcy remoteness, eligible cover assets, segregation, coverage and liquidity buffers. Article 17 confines extendable maturity to objective triggers and specifies its effect on claims and priority. Prerequisite: distinguish the issuer's unsecured estate from the cover-pool estate and map asset collections, overcollateralisation and extension dates. Translate the relevant national implementation and prospectus into a two-source recovery and liquidity waterfall, rather than assigning a generic bank recovery. Stress issuer default, cover-pool deterioration and payment deferral together. The Directive establishes an EU framework, not identical national collateral eligibility, supervisory practice or a quoted fair spread.}

\ExtendedNote{depth-preferred-ias32}{Classifies a preferred instrument by its contractual obligation to deliver cash or another financial asset, rather than by its name. Redemption obligations and issuer discretion over dividends can therefore place superficially similar preferred shares on different sides of the liability/equity boundary. Prerequisite: read dividend, redemption and liquidation clauses separately. Reconcile accounting classification with capital-structure valuation and issuer financial statements. \section{Synthetic risk transfer}\label{catalogue-section-12-6}
\label{sec:depth-srt}
\ExtendedNote{subject-33}{In a synthetic risk transfer (SRT), the bank normally keeps the loans and transfers defined credit losses on a reference portfolio through protection. Analyze the attachment and detachment points, loss settlement, retained senior and junior risk, protection provider, funded collateral and investor financing as one trade. Regulatory capital relief must be tested under the relevant jurisdiction's rules and supervisory process.}
\href{catalogue_extended_notes.html\#subject-33}{Subject context and qualifications}.
\CatalogueEntry{depth-srt-bcbs2026}{Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, \href{https://www.bis.org/bcbs/publ/d607.pdf}{Synthetic Risk Transfers}}{Not specified}{Report / research note}{BCBS report, February 2026; public PDF}{Surveys synthetic protection on loans that remain with the originating bank, tranche design, capital relief, protection sellers and supervisory concerns. Prerequisite: portfolio loss distributions, credit derivatives and securitisation capital treatment. Use the report to build a reference-pool-to-tranche bridge and a checklist for retained risk, counterparty exposure and capital recognition. It is a cross-jurisdictional supervisory survey, not an individual bank's approved relief, complete transaction database or model for a quoted tranche premium.}{}

Model tranche losses and protection payments separately from collateral and counterparty losses; stress investor repo funding and protection rollover. The article distinguishes the broad EU/UK regulatory phrase ``significant risk transfer'' from the narrower synthetic mechanism. Its market aggregates and illustrative structures do not resolve the economics of a private deal.}

\ExtendedNote{depth-srt-ecb-microdata}{Uses transaction and loan-level data to study which loans enter SRT reference portfolios, how issuing banks redeploy capital and how monitoring changes after transfer. It tests the claim that regulatory capital relief equals complete economic risk transfer. Prerequisite: understand endogenous portfolio selection and the bank's retained first- or senior-loss exposure. Use its evidence to challenge static capital-benefit estimates and to compare bank and investor incentives after closing. The empirical identification and confidential data cover the observed market and period; the working paper is not a universal causal parameter for future issuers or a public deal-level loss model.}

\section{Mortgage valuation and securitisation}\label{catalogue-section-12-8}
\label{sec:gap-securitised-credit}
\label{sec:depth-securitisation-waterfalls}
Read collateral behaviour, servicing incentives and deal waterfalls together. Residential prepayment, commercial-property refinancing, consumer-loan selection and CLO reinvestment generate different cash-flow risks. OAS and tranche spreads remain conditional on the selected model and documents.
\ExtendedNote{subject-36}{Start with dated collateral cash flows, then apply the legal allocation of fees, interest, principal and losses at every payment date. Triggers make the waterfall state-dependent: a single static subordination percentage cannot reproduce a switch from pro rata to sequential pay, a diverted cash flow or an early-amortisation event. Read this route with the prepayment and private-label servicing entries in Section~\ref{sec:gap-securitised-credit}.}
\href{catalogue_extended_notes.html\#subject-36}{Subject context and qualifications}.
\CatalogueEntry{exp-vickery-wright-tba-mbs}{James Vickery and Joshua Wright, \href{https://www.newyorkfed.org/research/epr/2013/1212vick.html}{TBA Trading and Liquidity in the Agency MBS Market}; \href{https://www.newyorkfed.org/research/economists/medialibrary/media/research/epr/2013/EPRvol19no1.pdf}{2013 full EPR issue}}{Advanced}{Research paper}{Federal Reserve Bank of New York Economic Policy Review 19(1), 1--18, May 2013; predecessor Staff Report 468 first August 2010, revised 2014. Cite the 2013 EPR article as the selected version.}{Explains the agency MBS to-be-announced convention, where a forward trade specifies eligible pool characteristics but leaves exact deliverables to later allocation, and estimates a material liquidity benefit around the crisis. The estimated 2009--2010 liquidity benefit is historical and the government guarantee alone is not the full explanation; prepayment, delivery eligibility, dollar-roll and settlement details still require separate modelling.}{\href{catalogue_extended_notes.html\#exp-vickery-wright-tba-mbs}{Extended note}.}

\ExtendedNote{gap-sec-abs-asset-disclosure}{Specifies standardized, tagged asset-level disclosure for covered public securitizations, including residential and commercial mortgages, auto loans and leases, and debt securities. This is the route from a generic ABS cash-flow model to fields a researcher can actually obtain in prospectus and ongoing XML exhibits. \ExtendedNote{depth-sec-rmbs-screening}{Uses a credit-score threshold affecting ease of securitisation to identify weaker screening and subsequent default among comparable US subprime loans. \ExtendedNote{evidence-rithm-advances}{Connects borrower delinquency and foreclosure duration to advances, reimbursement priority and funding. Non-agency advances generally rank ahead of trust note payments; recoverability may depend on loan/property proceeds, pool collections and servicer compliance. Note 5 distinguishes principal/interest, escrow and foreclosure advances, provisions and write-offs. Prerequisite: servicing cash flows versus credit-loss allocation. Use to challenge the assumption that priority guarantees full or prompt recovery. Advancing obligations and age-dependent financing eligibility can increase cash needs even before ultimate losses are known. Servicer-advance investments and advances receivable have different economics; discount rates, portfolio averages and accounting provisions are not realised security returns. This US issuer portfolio does not replace a particular CMBS PSA or monthly collateral tape.}

\ExtendedNote{subject-37}{Commercial mortgage-backed securities (CMBS) require property and whole-loan detail as well as bond-priority code. An appraisal reduction can change advances and interest timing before a realised collateral loss; special servicing, companion loans and control rights can change the workout path. Use the CMBS property-liquidity model as the economic layer.}
\href{catalogue_extended_notes.html\#subject-37}{Subject context and qualifications}.

\ExtendedNote{depth-sec-cmbs-2025-deal}{Specifies a liquidated-loan proceeds order after advances and expenses, treatment of interest not advanced because of appraisal reductions, and special-servicer sale and whole-loan constraints. The 17 March Form 10-D reports four 30-plus-day delinquencies (8.37\% of pool balance), no loans/REOs with losses and average net loss N/A. Indexed official Exhibit 99.1 text shows certificate interest \$4,122,095.20, principal \$248,015.80 and total fees \$10,952.80 for that distribution; interest plus principal equals the reported \$4,370,111.00 available distribution amount. These are observed monthly flows, distinct from account balances and ultimate recoveries. The exhibit also lists interest paid or advanced \$3,858,151.05 and an interest-reserve withdrawal \$274,896.93; the indexed line does not split paid from advanced interest. Full exhibit, ABS-EE XML, definitive PSA and 424B2 were not retrieved, so advances, fees and bond allocations cannot be independently reconciled into a validated waterfall. This one deal is not a universal CMBS rule.}

\chapter{FX, macro and regional markets}\label{catalogue-chapter-13}
Connect cross-asset premia, macro regimes and news, exchange-rate determination, currency premia and hedging to regional access, settlement and data. A country label is not a substitute for an instrument and contract specification.

\subsection{Cross-asset style premia and factor timing}\label{catalogue-section-13-1-sub-cross-asset-style-premia-and-factor-timing}
Value, momentum, carry and defensive premia measured across equity indices, bonds, currencies and commodities, and the evidence on timing them. Core cross-asset papers, among them \hyperlink{alpha-value}{Value and Momentum Everywhere}, \hyperlink{alpha-carry}{Carry} and \hyperlink{alpha-bab}{Betting Against Beta}, are in Sections~\ref{catalogue-section-2-1} and~\ref{catalogue-section-10-1}.

\section{Macro regimes, inflation and the stock--bond correlation}\label{catalogue-section-13-regimes}
How asset classes and styles behave across growth, inflation and volatility regimes, how to model regime changes for allocation, and what drives the sign of the stock--bond correlation. Regime-switching econometrics is in Section~\ref{catalogue-section-2-4}; inflation-linked bonds and real yields are in Section~\ref{catalogue-section-11-3}.
\Needspace{8\baselineskip}
\subsection{Regime models and macro sensitivities}\label{catalogue-section-13-regimes-sub-regime-models-and-macro-sensitivities}

\section{Macro news, announcements and nowcasting}\label{catalogue-section-13-macro-news}
How prices respond to scheduled macro releases and central-bank decisions, how much return is earned around them, and how to track the economy in real time. \section{Currency risk premia and factors}\label{catalogue-section-13-2}
Carry, momentum, value and dollar factors, the risk-based and equilibrium explanations offered for them, and the theory linking exchange rates to stochastic discount factors. Covered-interest-parity and funding evidence is in Section~\ref{catalogue-section-13-fx-cip}; option-implied and crash-risk evidence is in Section~\ref{catalogue-section-13-fx-volatility}.

\ExtendedNote{exp-bis-2026-carry-policy-transmission}{Shows that exchange-rate responses to a monetary-policy shock depend on pre-carry positioning: large shorts in funding currencies can unwind and amplify appreciation after tightening. This adds a state-dependent transmission channel to the UIP tests, currency factor papers, and carry-crash reading; it is useful for event stress, hedge sizing, and distinguishing direct rate effects from positioning feedback. Positions and policy surprises are imperfectly observed, so the result should not be converted into a deterministic FX timing rule or assumed to hold uniformly across currencies.}

\section{Covered interest parity, the cross-currency basis and dollar funding}\label{catalogue-section-13-fx-cip}
How covered-interest-parity deviations are measured, why the cross-currency basis has persisted since 2008, and how hedging demand, dealer balance sheets, regulation and central-bank swap lines set the price of synthetic dollar funding. Hedging demand from investors is also covered in Section~\ref{catalogue-section-13-fx-hedging}.
\CatalogueEntry{gap-cip}{Wenxin Du, Alexander Tepper and Adrien Verdelhan, \href{https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/jofi.12620}{Deviations from Covered Interest Rate Parity}}{Research}{Research paper}{Journal of Finance 73(3), 915--957, 2018.}{Documents persistent covered-interest-parity deviations and their relationship to quarter-end bank balance-sheet constraints. It provides an empirical foundation for interpreting cross-currency basis as more than a mechanical curve-fitting residual. Reproduce contract dates, collateral, credit exposure and balance-sheet costs before calling a spread arbitrage; the paper's findings do not imply that every investor can finance and scale the same trade.}{\href{catalogue_extended_notes.html\#gap-cip}{Extended note}.}

\ExtendedNote{gap-cip}{Documents persistent covered-interest-parity deviations and their relationship to quarter-end bank balance-sheet constraints. It provides an empirical foundation for interpreting cross-currency basis as more than a mechanical curve-fitting residual. Use it when comparing cash funding with FX-swap funding or assessing apparently profitable hedged bond trades. Reproduce contract dates, collateral, credit exposure and balance-sheet costs before calling a spread arbitrage; the paper's findings do not imply that every investor can finance and scale the same trade.}

\section{Currency hedging for international portfolios}\label{catalogue-section-13-fx-hedging}
How much of a foreign portfolio's currency exposure to hedge, over which horizon and at what cost, and how hedging demand feeds back into exchange rates and the cross-currency basis. Basis and funding evidence is in Section~\ref{catalogue-section-13-fx-cip}.
\CatalogueEntry{ma-black-1989}{Fischer Black, \href{https://doi.org/10.2469/faj.v45.n4.16}{``Universal Hedging: Optimizing Currency Risk and Reward in International Equity Portfolios''}}{Research}{Research paper}{Financial Analysts Journal, 45(4), 16--22 (1989); DOI 10.2469/faj.v45.n4.16.}{Derives a universal currency-hedge ratio for international equity investors who share common views, in liquid markets without barriers to international investing. \section{FX options, fixes, execution and settlement}\label{catalogue-section-13-3}
\label{sec:exp-fx-structure}
\label{sec:gap-fx-specialist}
The FX market combines bilateral credit, dealer internalisation, aggregators and venue-specific execution rules. Read these institutional sources with the mathematical execution models and current counterparty disclosures.
\ExtendedNote{subject-64}{Follow quote conventions and smile construction with basis economics and institutional hedging demand. Use the global survey and regional evidence to distinguish deliverable, non-deliverable and domestic-market exposures, then connect to the wholesale execution and settlement readings.}

\section{Emerging-market currencies, exchange-rate regimes and intervention}\label{catalogue-section-13-fx-em}
De facto exchange-rate regimes, pegs, floors and target zones, currency crises, foreign-exchange intervention and capital-flow measures, non-deliverable and offshore markets, and the dollar's role in the global financial cycle. Capital flows are in Section~\ref{catalogue-section-13-capital-flows}, local-currency government bonds in Section~\ref{catalogue-section-13-em-bonds} and country market-access rules in Section~\ref{catalogue-section-13-4}.

\section{International equity integration, diversification and home bias}\label{catalogue-section-13-intl-integration}
Whether equity markets are priced globally or locally: international asset-pricing models with investment barriers and segmentation, measures of integration and comovement, contagion tests, long-run international return histories and their survivorship, and explanations of home bias. Country factor evidence is in Section~\ref{catalogue-section-13-global-factors}; emerging and frontier markets are in Section~\ref{catalogue-section-13-em-equity}.

\section{Global equity factors, country selection and return predictability}\label{catalogue-section-13-global-factors}
Value, momentum, profitability, investment, liquidity and volatility premia outside the United States; global, local and partially segmented factor models; country-level momentum, reversal and value; and cross-country lead--lag predictability. US factor evidence is in Section~\ref{catalogue-section-10-1}.

\section{Cross-listings, dual listings and asynchronous trading}\label{catalogue-section-13-cross-listing}
Why firms list abroad and what cross-listing does to value, liquidity and price discovery; ADR and dual-listed-company parity and the limits to arbitrage; return and volatility transmission across non-overlapping trading hours; and stale prices in international funds and country ETFs.

\section{International capital flows and benchmark-driven investors}\label{catalogue-section-13-capital-flows}
Push and pull drivers of capital flows, gross-flow episodes, daily custodian and mutual-fund flow evidence, benchmark and index-rebalancing effects, the spillovers of US monetary policy to emerging markets, and nationality-based restatements of cross-border holdings. The global financial cycle and the dollar are in Section~\ref{catalogue-section-13-fx-em}.

\section{Emerging-market local-currency government bonds}\label{catalogue-section-13-em-bonds}
Original sin and its partial redemption, the development and investor base of local-currency government bond markets, the effects of foreign holdings and index rebalancing on yields, liquidity and volatility, and the currency and duration risks behind flows. Sovereign default and local-currency credit risk are in Section~\ref{catalogue-section-11-4}; China's bond market is in Section~\ref{catalogue-section-13-4-sub-china-and-emerging-market-equities}.

\ExtendedNote{depth-eme-liquidity}{Links investor composition and hedge-market depth to bond bid--ask spreads and their recovery after shocks, using local projections and a panel of 16 EMEs through 2023. Provides a common empirical framework for the India, China, ASEAN, Latin America and South Africa paths without assuming identical market structures. Read after market microstructure and panel inference. Quoted five-year spreads, one-year mean-reversion estimates and selected stress windows measure particular dimensions of liquidity; they are not full executable depth. \ExtendedNote{depth-india-rbi-settlement}{The RBI maps G-sec/repo, FX and interest-rate-derivative trading and the sequence of primary auctions, secondary clearing and cash settlement; it documents non-resident participation and intraday funding frictions. \ExtendedNote{evidence-india-april-sequence}{27 March: ADs' end-of-business-day NOP-INR in the onshore deliverable market capped at USD 100 million; compliance no later than 10 April. 1 April, immediately: no INR NDDCs to resident/nonresident users (excluding ADs); no rebooking INR derivatives cancelled after issuance; no related-party INR FX derivatives. Deliverable hedges remained subject to the stated genuine-hedge/no-offsetting-NDDC condition. 20 April, immediately: Circular 07 expressly withdraws Circular 03's instructions, replacing them with a related-party INR derivative prohibition except cancellation/rollover of contracts and specified back-to-back transactions with non-related nonresident users. Related parties follow Ind AS 24/IAS 24 or equivalent standards. The March cap was not withdrawn. Use dated regimes for historical execution studies; neither the cap nor April user restriction is a universal notional cap or ban on all interbank NDDCs.}

\ExtendedNote{evidence-india-june-exclusions}{8 June permits AD Category-I banks to exclude swap positions from eligible FCNR(B), ECB and OFCB funding for the March cap. 23 June partially modifies this: banks shall exclude positions from the related hedged transactions both for March-cap compliance and net overnight open-position computation under the Master Direction. Prerequisite: match the hedge to eligible funding; this is not a general cap repeal. S-56 covers qualifying 3--5-year FCNR(B) deposits mobilised 8 June--30 September, with swaps available through 16 October 2026. S-57 covers specified PSU ECB drawdowns and bank OFCB inflows through 31 December 2026, with swaps through 15 January 2027; maturity and refinancing/option exclusions apply. As of 4 October, distinguish the elapsed deposit mobilisation window from the swap window and continuing eligible positions. No wider permission follows from a consolidation's omission.}

\ExtendedNote{depth-africa-imf-funding}{Compares Eurobond, syndicated-loan and domestic local-currency channels; sections III--V study dollar/global-rate drivers of spreads and the role of non-resident investors in local debt. It makes a sovereign's currency of funding and refinancing calendar an explicit part of spread analysis, rather than attributing all yield differences to a region label. Read with \hyperlink{gap-global-macro-database}{macro data}, then country debt offices. The authors' normal-period ``African premium'' result is model and sample dependent; IMF working papers are research, not Fund policy. Domestic-bond records and FX hedges are uneven across countries, so a pooled regional regression is not a tradable security list.}

\ExtendedNote{gapclose-nigeria-ndf-rollover}{MB-33 introduced rollover treatment for foreign portfolio investment hedges, requiring identical amount and tenor and combined tenor no longer than 12 months, with booking within five business days after the first contract matures. \chapter{Commodities and energy}\label{catalogue-chapter-14}
Storage, location, delivery and operating constraints shape commodity valuation. Power, freight, weather and carbon contracts require their own exposure and settlement definitions. Separate sections cover the theory of storage, hedging, options and real options, financialisation, commodity allocation and index products, crude oil, oil supply and demand shocks and forecasting, oil shocks and the macroeconomy, oil and asset markets, natural gas markets, electricity market design, short-term power markets, contract design and delivery, price discovery, trading firms and margin stress, spot price assessment and benchmarks, spatial arbitrage, price cycles, long-run prices, price stabilisation and trade policy, carbon allowance prices and derivatives, carbon pass-through and leakage, and voluntary carbon credits.
\Needspace{13\baselineskip}
\section{Storage, futures curves and physical options}\label{catalogue-section-14-1}
\label{sec:exp-commodities}
\label{sec:gap-physical-commodities}
Physical delivery, non-storability, location, weather and operating constraints can dominate a purely financial factor model. These specialist readings complement the broad commodity and trend-following entries.
\ExtendedNote{subject-43}{Extend the power and storage foundations to storable fuels, metals and crops. Progress from inventory economics to multi-factor pricing and operational options, then official physical data. Delivery grade, location, seasonality, transport and capacity determine which curve spreads can be captured.}
\href{catalogue_extended_notes.html\#subject-43}{Subject context and qualifications}.
\Needspace{8\baselineskip}

\ExtendedNote{exp-bessembinder-lemmon-power-forward}{Builds equilibrium forward pricing and hedging around electricity's limited storability, volatile spot prices, and demand-dependent skew rather than a conventional inventory carry equation. It makes a direct physical-market distinction for institutional commodity programs: the sign and magnitude of power forward premia vary with expected load and demand variance, with summer risk in the original evidence. The analysis is based on historical US power markets; current renewable penetration, nodal congestion, weather forecasts, caps, and local market design can change the premium and hedge effectiveness.}

\ExtendedNote{exp-flottmann-forward-power-hedging}{Models how off-market contracts for difference supporting renewable generation can withdraw hedge supply from an energy-only electricity forward market, leaving retailers more exposed to volatile spot prices. This extends the classic Bessembinder--Lemmon forward-premium reading to today's physical hedge capacity and policy-design problem, where a utility or power book must track contract tenor, shape, credit, and volume as well as price. The analysis is grounded in Australia's National Electricity Market; its forward-shortage mechanism and proposed recycling design should be assessed against each jurisdiction's contract and capacity arrangements.}

\ExtendedNote{exp-uniejewski-ziel-probabilistic-power}{Embeds probabilistic load, wind, and solar forecasts into parsimonious and LASSO day-ahead electricity-price models, finding that extreme forecast quantiles matter and improve error metrics over point-input benchmarks in German EPEX data from 2015--2023. \section{Theory of storage and commodity term-structure models}\label{catalogue-section-14-storage-theory}
Why commodities are stored when futures prices lie below spot prices: convenience yield, the supply-of-storage curve, competitive storage with stock-outs, inventories and volatility, and one-, two-, three- and N-factor, seasonal and jump models of spot prices, convenience yields and forward curves. Contract and delivery evidence for individual commodities is in Section~\ref{catalogue-section-14-1}.
\CatalogueEntry{ec-kaldor-1939}{Nicholas Kaldor, \href{https://doi.org/10.2307/2967593}{``Speculation and Economic Stability''}}{Research}{Research paper}{Review of Economic Studies, 7(1), 1--27 (1939); DOI 10.2307/2967593.}{Classic analysis of when speculation stabilises prices. Its section on stocks introduces the convenience yield: holders of inventories accept a return below interest and carrying costs because stocks on hand let them meet unexpected demand, so spot can exceed futures while stocks are positive.}{}

\section{Commodity hedging and corporate risk management}\label{catalogue-section-14-hedging}
Minimum-variance, cross- and time-varying hedge ratios; rolling hedges of long-dated commitments and the Metallgesellschaft case; and evidence on which producers and consumers hedge, how they do it and whether it adds value.
\CatalogueEntry{ec-working-1953}{Holbrook Working, \href{https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-349-02693-7_3}{``Futures Trading and Hedging''}}{Research}{Book chapter}{American Economic Review 43(3), 314--343 (1953); reprint (DOI 10.1007/978-1-349-02693-7\_3) in B. A. Goss and B. S. Yamey (eds), The Economics of Futures Trading, Palgrave Macmillan, 68--82 (1976).}{Argues that the textbook picture of hedging as pure risk avoidance is misleading. Merchants and processors hedge mainly to profit from expected changes in the spot--futures basis and to make storage and pricing decisions on the basis, which makes hedging a form of arbitrage. The standard source for the "basis trading" view of commercial hedging.}{}

\section{Financialisation, speculation and index investing}\label{catalogue-section-14-financialisation}
Whether index investors and speculators changed commodity prices, volatility and correlations: the 2008 Senate testimony and CFTC survey that framed the debate, surveys, CFTC position data and their limits, storage-based and structural tests in oil, flow-based identification, models of financialisation, and its information and real effects. Commodity risk premia and factor strategies are in Section~\ref{catalogue-section-14-1}.

\ExtendedNote{physical-kilian-murphy-oil-2014}{Adds inventories to a structural oil-market model so shocks to speculative demand can be separated from flow demand and supply. The authors attribute the 2003--2008 surge mainly to global consumption growth rather than speculative trading or unexpectedly shrinking supply, while finding speculative shifts mattered in earlier episodes. This is valuable for scenario attribution and for resisting a single-cause futures-position narrative. \section{Commodity allocation, inflation hedging and index products}\label{catalogue-section-14-allocation}
Whether commodities belong in a multi-asset portfolio: diversification evidence in and out of sample, inflation hedging, commodity factor premia in the strategic mix, index rules and enhanced indices, futures-based ETFs, the price effects of index and ETF trading, and the USO case of April 2020. Risk premia and factor strategies are in Section~\ref{catalogue-section-14-1}; financialisation is in Section~\ref{catalogue-section-14-financialisation}.

Bills anchor low-risk portfolios (the minimum-risk portfolio has a mean real return of zero and a standard deviation of about 1 per cent), stocks have the highest mean and risk, and commodity futures are the only asset positively correlated with inflation, so adding them reaches any target real return with less risk. Published in 1982 in \emph{The Changing Roles of Debt and Equity in Financing U.S. Capital Formation}, 47--64.}{}

\section{Oil supply and demand shocks and oil-price forecasting}\label{catalogue-section-14-oil-shocks}
Identification of oil supply and demand shocks with structural VARs, sign restrictions, elasticity bounds and external instruments; measures of global real activity; and forecasting the real price of oil in real time with futures, product spreads, VARs and forecast combinations. Macroeconomic effects are in Section~\ref{catalogue-section-14-oil-macro} and asset-price effects in Section~\ref{catalogue-section-14-oil-assets}.

\section{Oil shocks, inflation and monetary policy}\label{catalogue-section-14-oil-macro}
How oil-price shocks affect output, consumption, inflation and inflation expectations; the breakdown, nonlinearity and asymmetry debates; and the role of monetary policy, from the 1970s to the 2021--22 inflation surge. Identification and forecasting are in Section~\ref{catalogue-section-14-oil-shocks}.

The correlation is statistically significant and not spurious even for 1948--72, suggesting oil shocks contributed to some recessions.}{}

\section{Natural gas markets, hub pricing and market integration}\label{catalogue-section-14-gas}
Hub price formation after open access and liberalisation, regional and international market integration, the link between gas and oil prices, shale-gas supply and the 2022 European supply shock, and the EU rules phasing out Russian gas. Storage valuation is in Section~\ref{catalogue-section-14-1} and LNG contracts in Section~\ref{catalogue-section-14-3}.

Member states had to file diversification plans by 1 March 2026.}{}

\CatalogueEntry{add-ftr-manual}{PJM Interconnection, \href{https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/documents/manuals/m06.ashx}{Manual 06: Financial Transmission Rights}}{Advanced}{Contract / specification / guidance}{PJM Manual 06, revision 35, effective 24 September 2026; operative market manual at the review date.}{Defines FTR obligations and options as financial claims on day-ahead nodal congestion-price differences, not physical transmission rights. After nodal-price foundations, calculate an hourly source-to-sink obligation payoff and option payoff, then reconcile auction price with realised congestion credits and any funding adjustment. Preserve product, path, MW, on/off-peak period and rule revision. \EntryRecency{add-ftr-manual}{Effective 24 September 2026; publication date not separately established.}{Revision 35; effective date 2026-09-24}{2026-10-04}{\href{https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/documents/manuals/m06.ashx}{Official manual, approval/effective dates and sections 1, 6--9}}{None}{Quarterly}
\ExtendedNote{add-ftr-manual}{Revision 35 is effective 24 September 2026. The manual states that FTRs are financial instruments and that holders need not deliver energy; an obligation can create a charge when the congestion-price difference reverses, whereas an option floors that hourly difference at zero. Its table of contents identifies auction credit rules in section 6, settlement in section 8 and simultaneous feasibility in section 9. Use an actual auction result, hourly day-ahead congestion components and monthly settlement statement to reproduce cash flow. The manual is a rules layer, not an empirical return series or a substitute for the applicable PJM tariff and credit documents.}

Use its tables to compare auction-implied congestion value with realised day-ahead congestion and holder payments after reading Manual 06. \Needspace{13\baselineskip}
\section{Electricity market design, renewables and market power}\label{catalogue-section-14-power-design}
Scarcity pricing, capacity mechanisms and resource adequacy; market power and the effect of forward contracts and vertical arrangements; reliability events and market-design reforms; and the market value of wind and solar, merit-order and cannibalisation effects and market design for high-renewable systems. Power contracts, storage services and transmission rights are in Section~\ref{catalogue-section-14-2}.
\CatalogueEntry{ec-joskow-2008}{Paul L. Joskow, \href{https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jup.2007.10.003}{``Capacity Payments in Imperfect Electricity Markets: Need and Design''}}{Research}{Research paper}{Utilities Policy, 16(3), 159--170 (2008); DOI 10.1016/j.jup.2007.10.003.}{Imperfections in energy-only wholesale markets leave generators with net revenues too low to support the least-cost capacity mix and the reliability consumers want ("missing money"). Better scarcity pricing helps but is unlikely to close the gap, so forward capacity obligations with auctions are needed; the paper also diagnoses the flaws of early US capacity payments.}{}

\section{Short-term power markets, balancing and flexibility}\label{catalogue-section-14-power-short-term}
Sequential day-ahead, intraday and balancing markets; intraday price formation, forecasting and optimal trading; imbalance pricing; negative prices; and the arbitrage value and equilibrium effects of storage, including Europe's 2025 move to 15-minute day-ahead products and ERCOT's real-time co-optimisation. Transmission rights and storage services are in Section~\ref{catalogue-section-14-2}.

Iberian market microdata support the predictions, and a structural model shows that with market power full arbitrage need not raise welfare: it lowers consumer costs but increases deadweight loss.}{}

\CatalogueEntry{add-lng-option}{A. Baba, A. Creti and O. Massol, \href{https://openaccess.city.ac.uk/id/eprint/24225/}{What Can Be Learned from the Free Destination Option in the LNG Imbroglio?}}{Research}{Research paper}{\emph{Energy Economics} 89, article 104764, 2020; university repository provides an author manuscript and abstract.}{Values an LNG supplier's destination flexibility by simulating regional gas-price paths and choosing the best shipping decision for each path. Separate the gross value of redirection from charter costs, contractual notices, export permissions and any foregone delivery commitment. \EntryRecency{add-lng-option}{2020}{Published journal article; accessible author manuscript}{2026-10-04}{\href{https://openaccess.city.ac.uk/id/eprint/24225/}{University repository bibliographic record and abstract}}{None}{Annual}
\ExtendedNote{add-lng-option}{The City Research Online record identifies the 2020 journal article, DOI 10.1016/j.eneco.2020.104764, and an author-manuscript version. Its abstract supports the threshold-regime price model, Monte Carlo path simulation and optimal shipping-decision method. Treat the paper as a valuation framework. In a practical replication, specify the option holder, nomination date, alternative port, boil-off and charter exposure, and compare exercise with the actual sale-and-purchase agreement. The paper's claim of profitable destination flexibility is sample- and assumption-dependent; it should not be copied as a standing arbitrage spread.}
\CatalogueEntry{add-lng-contract}{Corpus Christi Liquefaction and Cheniere Marketing International, \href{https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1693317/000169331726000003/exhibit1046cch2025form10k.htm}{LNG Sale and Purchase Agreement (FOB), Exhibit 10.46}}{Advanced}{Contract / specification / guidance}{Executed 25 February 2026; SEC-filed affiliated-party FOB agreement; selected clauses inspected in full text.}{A concrete contract for turning LNG price spreads into exercise rights and obligations. Section 3.3 permits resale and destination choice subject to export-authorisation conditions; section 5.7 permits scheduled-cargo cancellation by a specified notice deadline and a fee equal to the indexed FOB fixed component times scheduled quantity. Section 9.1 prices delivered LNG from 1.15 times Henry Hub plus that fixed component. Build a cargo decision tree across lifting, diversion and cancellation, adding freight and downstream commitments. This is an affiliated-party agreement; its economics and flexibility cannot be treated as representative third-party terms or observed arbitrage profit.}{\href{catalogue_extended_notes.html\#add-lng-contract}{Extended note}.}
\EntryRecency{add-lng-contract}{Agreement executed/effective 25 February 2026; SEC filing date is separate and not established here.}{Executed agreement, Exhibit 10.46}{2026-10-04}{\href{https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1693317/000169331726000003/exhibit1046cch2025form10k.htm}{SEC filed executed agreement: recitals and sections 3.3, 5.7, 9.1, 26.1}}{None}{Annual}
\ExtendedNote{add-lng-contract}{The executed exhibit names Corpus Christi Liquefaction as seller and Cheniere Marketing International as buyer, effective 25 February 2026. Section 3.3 allows destination choice subject to export authorisation; section 5.7 sets a cancellation notice by day 17 of the month two months before the delivery-window month and a fee of FOB Xy times scheduled cargo quantity. Section 9.1 gives contract sales price as 1.15 times Henry Hub plus FOB Xy. It references a downstream Orlen SPA, so a group's apparent route option may be constrained elsewhere. Do not infer realised exercise, realised profit or third-party market terms from the filed contract alone.}

\section{Futures contract design, delivery and manipulation}\label{catalogue-section-14-delivery}
Why some futures contracts succeed; how much is delivered and what the grade, timing and location options embedded in delivery are worth; convergence failures in grain futures and storage-rate remedies; corners, squeezes and manipulation of the delivery process; and the principles, storage-infrastructure practices and position limits that govern physically delivered contracts.

\section{Price discovery and fundamental information}\label{catalogue-section-14-information}
Where commodity prices are discovered across cash and futures markets and across exchanges; how futures react to weather, USDA crop reports, EIA inventory reports and analyst forecasts; and what satellite and ship-tracking data add to official statistics.

\section{Spot price assessment and benchmarks}\label{catalogue-section-14-spot-benchmarks}
How spot commodity prices are assessed and published: price reporting agencies and their oversight, auction benchmarks for precious metals, the design of fixings that traders can manipulate, the move from annual contract to index pricing, and contract pricing where spot markets are thin.
\CatalogueEntry{sp-imsirovic-2021}{Adi Imsirovic, \href{https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-030-71718-6}{\emph{Trading and Price Discovery for Crude Oils: Growth and Development of International Oil Markets}}}{Advanced}{Book / monograph}{Springer International Publishing (2021); DOI 10.1007/978-3-030-71718-6.}{How crude oil prices are set. Most oil is never traded: its value is fixed by a few benchmark grades and baskets---Brent, WTI, Dubai and Oman---traded as physical and paper barrels in volumes many times world output, which separates price makers from price takers. Separate chapters cover the Brent, Dubai--Oman and WTI benchmarks; earlier ones trace oil pricing from the early US market through the eras of the majors and OPEC, and a late chapter draws lessons from the 2020 pandemic.}{}

\section{Commodity price cycles, comovement and macro drivers}\label{catalogue-section-14-price-cycles}
Surveys and current outlooks of primary commodity markets; the dating of booms and slumps; common factors in commodity prices and their links to global activity, real interest rates and the dollar; and forecasts of commodity spot prices.

\section{Long-run commodity prices and resource scarcity}\label{catalogue-section-14-long-run}
Tests of the Hotelling rule, the Prebisch--Singer hypothesis of declining relative commodity prices, long-run trends, supercycles and boom--bust episodes, and the supply responses and market power that shape long-run prices.

\section{Price stabilisation, public stocks and trade policy}\label{catalogue-section-14-stabilisation}
Buffer stocks, price bands and international commodity agreements analysed with the storage model; strategic oil reserves and coordinated stock releases; and export restrictions and insulating trade policy in the food price spikes of 2007--08 and 2022.
\CatalogueEntry{sp-gouel-wright-2026}{Christophe Gouel and Brian D. Wright, \href{https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-resource-112624-121752}{``Storage and the Economics of Commodity Price Stabilization''}}{Advanced}{Research paper}{Annual Review of Resource Economics, 18(1), 63--87 (2026); DOI 10.1146/annurev-resource-112624-121752.}{Reassesses price stabilisation through the rational-expectations storage model. In frictionless markets private storage already smooths prices efficiently, so public intervention needs market or endowment failures, common in low-income agricultural markets. Optimal state-contingent policies are complex and crowd out private storage; narrow price bands or storage subsidies approximate them, subsidies more efficiently. Storage can support prices in open economies with high trade costs, export controls insulate domestic prices but are non-cooperative, and the redistribution involved far exceeds the efficiency gains.}{}

\ExtendedNote{carbon-rubin-banking-1996}{Derives permit-price and emissions paths when firms may bank and borrow allowances, and compares that setting with banking only. It provides the intertemporal economic logic behind an allowance's inventory value and explains why an ETS curve depends on future caps and compliance choices, not conventional commodity warehousing. Applying it to any live program requires its exact borrowing restrictions, vintage fungibility, reserve rules, and expected policy changes. The continuous-time least-cost benchmark abstracts from market power, uncertain enforcement, transaction costs, and political redesign.}

\section{Carbon allowance prices, derivatives and market participants}\label{catalogue-section-14-carbon-prices}
Allowance price drivers and structural breaks, stochastic and equilibrium models of allowance prices, futures, options, convenience yields and price discovery, and the role of banks and other financial participants. Cap-and-trade design is in Section~\ref{catalogue-section-14-5}.
\CatalogueEntry{ec-hintermann-2010}{Beat Hintermann, \href{https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jeem.2009.07.002}{``Allowance Price Drivers in the First Phase of the EU ETS''}}{Research}{Research paper}{Journal of Environmental Economics and Management, 59(1), 43--56 (2010); DOI 10.1016/j.jeem.2009.07.002.}{In Phase I of the EU ETS the allowance price rose above 30 euros and then collapsed to almost zero by mid-2007. A structural model of the allowance price, relaxed to allow delayed adjustment, shows that prices were not driven by marginal abatement costs at first, but that this was largely corrected after 2005 emissions were reported in April 2006.}{}

\ExtendedNote{carbon-ice-eua-futures}{Defines a physically delivered European Union allowance futures contract, its eligible allowance, lot and delivery-account mechanics, and listed expiries. It is the operational bridge from EU ETS policy to a hedge or carbon basis trade: a December futures curve is a claim on the specified deliverable allowance, subject to exchange and registry timing, rather than a generic ton of avoided emissions. Cross-hedges against a company's actual compliance need must consider jurisdiction, surrender calendar, collateral, registry access, and the contract's current rulebook.}

\CatalogueEntry{carbon-balmford-permanence-2023}{Andrew Balmford, Srinivasan Keshav, Frank Venmans, et al., \href{https://doi.org/10.1038/s41558-023-01815-0}{Realizing the Social Value of Impermanent Carbon Credits}; \href{https://anil.recoil.org/papers/2023-ncc-permanence}{Author-hosted abstract and PDF}}{Research}{Research paper}{Nature Climate Change 13, 1172--1178, November 2023 issue; online 30 October 2023}{Frames a nature-based credit's permanence as additional climate benefit through time and includes the social cost of possible future reversal in valuation. \ExtendedNote{carbon-balmford-permanence-2023}{Frames a nature-based credit's permanence as additional climate benefit through time and includes the social cost of possible future reversal in valuation. That turns a binary permanent-versus-temporary label into a time path requiring monitoring and conservative estimates. It is especially relevant where wildfire, disease, or management changes could release stored carbon. \chapter{Private capital}\label{catalogue-chapter-15}
Separate security underwriting from fund performance, commitment pacing and financing. Illiquidity, selection, contractual priority and access affect reported returns.
\Needspace{13\baselineskip}
\section{Private equity, venture capital and performance}\label{catalogue-section-15-1}
\label{sec:gap-private-real}
\label{sec:gap-private-equity}
Start with deal and fund economics, then cash-flow benchmarking, risk adjustment, manager selection and secondary transactions. IRR, TVPI, PME and alpha answer different questions; commitment pacing and access constraints belong alongside reported returns.
\Needspace{8\baselineskip}
\subsection{Fund performance, persistence and secondaries}\label{catalogue-section-15-1-sub-fund-performance-persistence-and-secondaries}

\ExtendedNote{pe-braun-manager-skill-2026}{Links PE deals to individual managers and measures value creation in dollars of NPV as well as relative returns. The paper finds that relative returns decline with scale while NPV can rise, and that firms direct more capital to skilled managers. For diligence, distinguish a manager’s percentage return from value added at implementable scale and ask who made the deals. NPV depends on discount-rate choices and deal attribution; observing internal allocation does not reveal what an outside LP can access.}

\section{Fund commitments, financing and liquidity}\label{catalogue-section-15-3}
\label{sec:depth-private-funds}
\ExtendedNote{subject-71}{An LP controls commitments, not the date of calls or exits. Forecast unfunded commitments, NAV, distributions and liquid reserves jointly, and distinguish portfolio realizations from cash delivered by a subscription or NAV facility. Read the \hyperref[sec:gap-private-equity]{fund-return path} first.}
\href{catalogue_extended_notes.html\#subject-71}{Subject context and qualifications}.

\ExtendedNote{depth-pe-luxenberg-2022}{Models uncertain returns, calls and distributions as a stochastic system and selects liquid holdings and new commitments in successive periods. Read after Takahashi--Alexander to understand why an LP controls commitments rather than its current private weight, and why liquid reserves must meet high-probability calls. \CatalogueEntry{add-interval-mechanics}{U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, \href{https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/general-resources/news-alerts/alerts-bulletins/investor-bulletins/investor-bulletin-interval-funds}{Investor Bulletin: Interval Funds}}{Advanced}{Contract / specification / guidance}{SEC investor-education bulletin dated 25 September 2020; explanatory staff material, not binding rule text.}{Explains the liquidity mechanics of an interval-fund wrapper around illiquid assets. Repurchase offers occur at disclosed intervals; the fund generally offers to buy 5--25\% of shares, and oversubscription can lead to pro rata fulfilment. Shareholders accept before the later NAV pricing date, so requested liquidity, paid cash and realised sale price need separate dates. Use the bulletin to stress a private-credit or real-asset allocation with simultaneous investor requests, limited liquid assets and valuation lags. Read the chosen fund's prospectus and filings for its actual interval, fees, proration and suspension terms; this bulletin is education, not the governing contract.}{\href{catalogue_extended_notes.html\#add-interval-mechanics}{Extended note}.}
\EntryRecency{add-interval-mechanics}{2020-09-25}{Investor bulletin, SEC staff educational material}{2026-10-04}{\href{https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/general-resources/news-alerts/alerts-bulletins/investor-bulletins/investor-bulletin-interval-funds}{SEC Investor.gov bulletin, repurchase timing, pro rata mechanics and legal-status disclaimer}}{None}{Annual}
\ExtendedNote{add-interval-mechanics}{The SEC bulletin describes interval funds as registered closed-end funds that continuously or periodically offer shares at NAV but repurchase only at specified intervals. It describes the usual 5--25\% offer range, pro rata treatment when requests exceed the offer and a repurchase price determined after the acceptance deadline. It also states that the bulletin reflects staff views and has no legal force. A research cash-flow model should therefore distinguish the rule, the fund's prospectus, tender acceptance, NAV pricing and payment. The 2026 modernization proposal below is a separate proposed change, not a description of operative law.}

Todorov, \href{https://www.bis.org/publications/bulletin-106-retail-investors-private-credit}{Retail Investors in Private Credit}}{Advanced}{Report / research note}{BIS Bulletin 106, 9 July 2025; published policy research on retail private-credit vehicles.}{Places the growth of retail-access vehicles around private credit in a wider liquidity and price-discovery setting. The bulletin focuses on business development companies and private-credit ETFs, and notes that secondary prices can diverge from reported NAV during stress. Read it beside interval-fund mechanics to distinguish a traded share-price discount from a fund's scheduled, capacity-limited repurchase at NAV. Trace a loan portfolio through the vehicle's valuation, financing and exit channels before comparing quoted performance. The bulletin's ETF observations are not evidence that interval-fund shares trade continuously or that every private-credit loan can be sold quickly.}{\href{catalogue_extended_notes.html\#add-interval-evidence}{Extended note}.}

\ExtendedNote{add-interval-evidence}{BIS Bulletin 106 was published 9 July 2025. Its key takeaways address BDC and ETF access, potential ETF price signals, and the possibility that a secondary loan market could erode characteristics of private credit. It is a policy-research layer, not a prospectus or regulatory rule for interval funds. Compare BDC, ETF, tender-offer and interval wrappers separately: each has different leverage, market-price discovery, NAV calculation and cash-exit mechanics. Use a particular vehicle's filings to test whether retail flow reaches underlying loans, secondary shares or only a controlled repurchase window.}
\CatalogueEntry{add-interval-proposal}{U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, \href{https://www.sec.gov/files/rules/proposed/2026/33-11444.pdf}{Interval Fund Modernization and Multiple Share Classes for Registered Closed-End Funds and BDCs}}{Advanced}{Contract / specification / guidance}{Proposed rule, Release 33-11444, issued 30 September 2026; proposal open for comment at the review date, not adopted law.}{The SEC proposes changes to rule 23c-3, including a regular monthly repurchase option, altered notice and liquidity-management requirements, and related closed-end-fund share-class disclosures. The release describes current 3-, 6- and 12-month intervals alongside proposed alternatives, making it a dated way to compare existing and possible future fund cash timing. Build two scenarios for a private-credit interval fund: current governing terms and proposed terms only if adopted. Check subsequent rulemaking before updating a live model. Its economic analysis and examples are regulatory arguments, not evidence that monthly liquidity has already become generally available.}{\href{catalogue_extended_notes.html\#add-interval-proposal}{Extended note}.}
\EntryRecency{add-interval-proposal}{2026-09-30}{Proposed rule, Release 33-11444 / File S7-2026-34}{2026-10-04}{\href{https://www.sec.gov/rules-regulations/2026/09/s7-2026-34}{SEC rulemaking docket and proposal status}; \href{https://www.sec.gov/files/rules/proposed/2026/33-11444.pdf}{Official proposed-rule PDF, summary and proposed rule 23c-3 amendments}}{None}{Quarterly}
\ExtendedNote{add-interval-proposal}{The SEC's official rulemaking page identifies Release 33-11444 and File S7-2026-34 as a proposed rule issued 30 September 2026. The proposal's table of amendments would add one-month periodic intervals and revise notice, repurchase-payment and liquidity provisions. The same PDF describes currently applicable requirements for context; keep those paragraphs distinct from proposed text. \ExtendedNote{depth-special-occ-trade-2018}{Maps documentary letters of credit, guarantees, acceptances, open-account financing, supply-chain finance and prepayments to their different obligors, documents and settlement steps. Read before comparing a short-dated trade receivable with a corporate loan: importer, issuing bank, exporter and collateral can fail at different points. Use to create a claim-level checklist for goods, invoice authenticity, transfer, sanctions, FX and collection timing. The supervisory booklet is not the actual UCP undertaking, receivable purchase agreement or legal opinion; program controls and jurisdiction determine enforceability and loss.}

\CatalogueEntry{evidence-trade-antras}{Pol Antr\`as and C. \ExtendedNote{evidence-trade-antras}{Models importer nonpayment against exporter nondelivery and compares cash in advance, open account and bank-intermediated terms. Evidence comes from one US food exporter's transactions across countries in 1996--2009. Prerequisite: working-capital financing, contracting and selection in observational data. The firm's transaction evidence is not a representative bank/fund portfolio. Publisher supplemental files are listed, but their contents were not validated here; a listed data supplement is not proof that raw proprietary transactions are public. No net investor-return estimate is imported.}
\CatalogueEntry{gapclose-trade-factoring-contract}{Majesco / HSBC Bank USA, \href{https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1626853/000157104917000496/t1700151_ex10-1.htm}{Receivables Purchase Agreement, Schedule and Standard Terms, Exhibit 10.1}}{Advanced}{Contract / specification / guidance}{Signed agreement dated 13 January 2017; SEC-filed full agreement, schedule, standard terms and signatures inspected. Historical U.S. services receivables case.}{An actual factoring contract with a USD 10 million limit, 90\% stated advance percentage, 40\% customer concentration percentage, 2\% margin and 0.2\% arrangement and annual review fees. The schedule expressly selects advances and non-notification, and declines HSBC credit-risk assumption. Build invoice-level eligibility, reserve, advance, interest, customer payment and recourse branches, including what happens if a receivable is disputed or overdue. The lender may reduce advance percentage or reserves, so the stated maximum is not guaranteed liquidity. This is domestic services factoring, not cross-border documentary credit or a representative trade-fund net return; historical LIBOR pricing needs replacement before a current model.}{\href{catalogue_extended_notes.html\#gapclose-trade-factoring-contract}{Extended note}.}
\EntryRecency{gapclose-trade-factoring-contract}{Agreement dated 13 January 2017; SEC exhibit filing in 2017.}{Executed contract with schedule and incorporated standard terms; historical LIBOR-linked pricing.}{2026-10-04}{\href{https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1626853/000157104917000496/t1700151_ex10-1.htm}{SEC Exhibit 10.1}, selected full sections, schedule and signatures.}{No later program amendment or replacement established in this review; do not use 2017 rates as current offers.}{Historical case; annual link/status check and transaction-specific current agreement review.}
\ExtendedNote{gapclose-trade-factoring-contract}{The signed Exhibit 10.1 names Majesco and affiliates as clients and HSBC Bank USA as factor. Its schedule sets U.S. approved accounts, a USD 10 million facility limit, 90\% advance percentage, 40\% concentration percentage, 2\% margin, 0.2\% arrangement and review fees, and no credit-risk assumption. Sections 2.1--2.3 transfer receivables; the schedule and standard terms decide which advances and losses remain with the seller. Standard Terms 3--5 make reserves and advances discretionary; receivable disputes and late payments matter. The exhibit's purchase-price worksheet is labelled illustrative and should be independently reconciled before reuse. This is one negotiated 2017 U.S. program, not an international-trade return panel, current SOFR agreement, or evidence of realised collections and investor net returns.}

\ExtendedNote{depth-special-occ-leasing-2023}{Separates lessee credit, contracted rentals, tax and accounting treatment, maintenance, off-lease time and unguaranteed residual value. Build an aircraft or equipment lease model with downtime, return conditions, remarketing cost and sale value after the final rental, rather than treating all lease cash as a fixed coupon. Stress tenant default and asset residual together; an aircraft engine or specialized machine is not interchangeable with generic equipment. The handbook is for supervised banks and does not provide current aircraft appraisal values, legal title, registry status or insurance for a particular asset.}
\CatalogueEntry{evidence-gavazza-leases}{Alessandro Gavazza, \href{https://agavazza.github.io/Papers/airliquidityJFE.pdf}{Asset Liquidity and Financial Contracts: Evidence from Aircraft Leases}}{Research}{Research paper}{\emph{Journal of Financial Economics} 95(1), 62--84, January 2010; author-hosted published text.}{Relates aircraft marketability to lease type, maturity and rental markups. Combines an April 2003 fleet cross-section and aircraft histories with appraised model/vintage prices and operating-lease rates for 1967--2003. The historical commercial data are not a verified freely reusable loan tape or a causal guarantee for today's aircraft.}{\href{catalogue_extended_notes.html\#evidence-gavazza-leases}{Extended note}.}

\ExtendedNote{evidence-gavazza-leases}{Relates aircraft marketability to lease type, maturity and rental markups. Combines an April 2003 fleet cross-section and aircraft histories with appraised model/vintage prices and operating-lease rates for 1967--2003. Prerequisite: lease versus secured-loan economics, fixed effects and appraisal measurement. Inform remarketing and residual-value scenarios, then compare the following actual lease. Broad fleet coverage does not make the appraisal panel realised investor returns: prices assume a cash sale by a non-bankrupt seller; capital-lease rates and many carrier credit variables are missing. The historical commercial data are not a verified freely reusable loan tape or a causal guarantee for today's aircraft.}

Inform residual-value and workout scenarios without assuming identical recovery across equipment classes or jurisdictions. Full journal/preprint equivalence, current equipment loss tapes and a representative investable net-return panel remain open.}
\CatalogueEntry{gapclose-equipment-lease-contract}{CHG-MERIDIAN U.S. Finance / CDF2 Holdings, \href{https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1173204/000093244011001123/ex10-3_283470.htm}{Master Equipment Lease and Schedule 001, Exhibit 10.3}}{Advanced}{Contract / specification / guidance}{Signed execution version dated 18 October 2011; SEC exhibit contains master lease, rider, one executed digital-cinema equipment schedule and signature counterparts.}{A contract-level equipment case with 618 scheduled units, a 66-month initial term, monthly rent of USD 216,300 for the first 15 months and USD 482,040 for months 16--66, plus a six-month mandatory renewal at the initial-term rate. Model the lessor's contracted receipts, funding, lessee/sublessee performance, loss and end-of-term option separately. The schedule's rent is not realised cash collection or investor IRR, and linked sale-leaseback, senior-credit and multiparty records need reconciliation.}{\href{catalogue_extended_notes.html\#gapclose-equipment-lease-contract}{Extended note}.}
\EntryRecency{gapclose-equipment-lease-contract}{Effective 18 October 2011; SEC-filed 2011 executed exhibit.}{Master Equipment Lease No. 8463 and signed Schedule 001; historical transaction.}{2026-10-04}{\href{https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1173204/000093244011001123/ex10-3_283470.htm}{SEC Exhibit 10.3}, master sections 2, 10--13, Schedule 001 and signatures.}{Related financing and later amendments not traced; not a current market quote.}{Historical case; verify related agreements and asset cash flows before a return exercise.}
\ExtendedNote{gapclose-equipment-lease-contract}{The 18 October 2011 master lease and Schedule 001 are signed by CHG-MERIDIAN and CDF2 Holdings. The schedule names Marcus Theatres as a permitted sublessee and states 618 units, 66 months and staged monthly rents of USD 216,300 then USD 482,040, with a six-month mandatory renewal. Section 2 addresses term and rent; section 10 specifies default remedies including a casualty-value formula and application of re-lease or sale proceeds. Schedule 001 ties purchase cost and possible variable rent to the related sale-leaseback and multiparty financing agreements. Appraisal terms affect end-of-term purchase value. Use the dated schedule for contractual, not collected, cash flows. Actual equipment acceptance dates, losses, residual sale prices, tax, fund fees and financing distributions were not reconciled.}

\CatalogueEntry{gapclose-pharma-royalty-contract}{PTC Therapeutics / Royalty Pharma, \href{https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1070081/000155837024002196/tmb-20231231xex10d48.htm}{2023 amended royalty purchase agreement}; \href{https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1070081/000110465926017575/tmb-20251231xex10d47.htm}{signed 2025 Amendment No. 2}; \href{https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1070081/000107008126000017/tmb-20260630x10q.htm}{June 2026 filing}}{Advanced}{Contract / specification / guidance}{Base agreement signed 18 October 2023, amended 17 June 2024 and 29 December 2025; 2025 amendment full text and June 2026 issuer accounting inspected.}{The executed chain shows why a royalty slice must be dated. The 2023 agreement split Evrysdi-related rights around a USD 1.3 billion assigned-payment cap and included seller put options; the signed December 2025 amendment transferred the remaining interest for USD 240 million upfront plus at most USD 60 million in contingent purchase-price payments. After that closing Royalty Pharma holds 100\% of the specified royalty, which the June 2026 10-Q confirms alongside USD 2.1 billion total funding. The agreement governs payment instructions, reports, reductions and enforcement; a licence payer's credit nonpayment is not automatically a seller true-up. \ExtendedNote{gapclose-pharma-royalty-contract}{The 2023 executed purchase agreement assigns slices of PTC's Evrysdi-related royalty, with buyer/seller percentages changing after the buyer receives USD 1.3 billion under the 2020 assigned royalty. The signed 29 December 2025 Amendment No. 2 replaces the seller's remaining 9.5111\% pre-cap / 16.6666\% post-cap share with 100\% buyer ownership, pays USD 240 million upfront, adds up to three contingent USD 20 million payments, and extends buyer-request rights over patent maintenance. \chapter{Property, infrastructure and natural-resource rights}\label{catalogue-chapter-16}
Property, projects and natural-resource rights generate different cash flows. Appraisal evidence, operating constraints and legal rights should remain visible in valuation.

NCREIF emphasizes that NTBI is equal-weighted, depends on the small subset that trades, omits hotels, and is not intended as a fund benchmark. Transaction selection, changing asset quality, and sparse sales require explicit treatment before interpreting a quarterly movement as the whole market.}

It is the vehicle-level counterpart to the property-level NPI, making leverage, cash balances, fund costs, and structure visible in comparisons. Use matching gross/net and leverage definitions when grading a manager. The index covers a defined group of diversified core funds, not value-add or closed-end vehicles, and periodic redemptions do not guarantee immediate cash liquidity.}{}

\section{Infrastructure and project finance}\label{catalogue-section-16-2}
\label{sec:gap-infrastructure}
\label{sec:depth-property-infra}
\ExtendedNote{subject-74}{Begin with ring-fenced project cash flows and risk allocation, then fund-level evidence, project databases and debt outcomes. Construction, demand, regulated tariffs and offtake contracts can dominate the generic asset-class label; direct assets and closed-end funds have different liquidity profiles.}
\href{catalogue_extended_notes.html\#subject-74}{Subject context and qualifications}.
Underwrite the lease, plant, contract or regulated concession first; then map that cash flow through construction, financing, refinancing and the fund vehicle. A property or infrastructure index cannot replace those layers.

Government guarantees and country risk matter to the funding package. The cases teach deal design, but their assumptions must be replaced with current project contracts, tariffs, capital costs, and jurisdiction-specific law before underwriting an actual asset.}{\href{catalogue_extended_notes.html\#infra-gatti-2023}{Extended note}.}

\ExtendedNote{infra-gatti-2023}{A practical foundation for valuing a ring-fenced infrastructure project from contracted and forecast cash flows rather than applying corporate multiples mechanically. Work through project characteristics, allocation of construction and operating risks, cash-flow valuation, financing, legal structure, and credit analysis, then test coverage ratios and downside cases in the book's examples. Government guarantees and country risk matter to the funding package. The cases teach deal design, but their assumptions must be replaced with current project contracts, tariffs, capital costs, and jurisdiction-specific law before underwriting an actual asset.}

\ExtendedNote{infra-andonov-kraussl-rauh-2021}{Tests the claim that infrastructure funds supply stable, countercyclical cash flows. Using institutional commitments and deals through June 2020, the authors find closed-end infrastructure funds have cash-flow volatility and cyclicality resembling private equity, depend on relatively quick exits, and offer weak risk-adjusted performance; public investors perform worse than private ones. This is essential when setting an allocation benchmark or liquidity model: project assets and fund wrappers create different exposures. The sample concerns mainly equity positions and historic fund structures, so it does not establish the same result for directly held project debt.}

\ExtendedNote{infra-world-bank-ppi-method}{Read this before using PPI financial-close counts or investment commitments as an infrastructure opportunity set. The database covers low- and middle-income public infrastructure with private operating risk; its commitment figure may combine public and private funding and is usually booked at financial close, not spread over realized annual capital spending. \ExtendedNote{depth-special-mei-moses-art-2002}{Builds repeat-sale evidence and tests whether expensive works outperform. Read as a method for separating repeat-sale price changes from broad claims that unique objects earn an illiquidity premium. A repeat-sales index is not a purchasable portfolio; compare the counterevidence in Etro--Stepanova before applying a masterpiece premium.}

\chapter{Insurance-linked investments}\label{catalogue-chapter-17}
Connect insured losses and demographic risks to triggers, payout timing, model uncertainty and capital release. Index and portfolio exposure need not coincide.
\Needspace{13\baselineskip}
\section{Catastrophe, mortality and longevity}\label{catalogue-section-17-1}
\label{sec:gap-insurance-linked}
\ExtendedNote{subject-77}{Begin with insurance-capital economics and contract taxonomy, then catastrophe pricing, trigger basis and current issuance. The longevity readings add population modelling and liability-matching risk. Modelled expected loss, market spread, realised loss and return after trapped capital must remain distinct.}

A quoted bond may embed liquidity, post-event uncertainty, collateral terms, and stale pricing alongside peril intensity, so the extracted parameter is not a pure physical event frequency. Thin trading and model changes should be treated explicitly when using it for daily valuation.}

\chapter{Digital assets}\label{catalogue-chapter-18}
Separate protocol design, spot trading, derivatives, financing, tokenisation and security. Recent mechanism research sits beside the market and contract foundations it extends; crypto spot markets and tokenised securities and real-world assets have their own sections. Event contracts and prediction markets, including on-chain venues, have their own chapter (Chapter~\ref{catalogue-chapter-18-events}).

\subsection{Leverage, liquidations and crypto lenders}\label{catalogue-section-18-1-sub-leverage-liquidations}
Exchange leverage and perpetual design, volatility transmission from leveraged venues, liquidation cascades and auto-deleveraging, the 2022 failures of centralised lenders, and US rules for crypto collateral at futures commission merchants.
\CatalogueEntry{cd-soska-2021}{Kyle Soska, Jin-Dong Dong, Alex Khodaverdian, Ariel Zetlin-Jones, Bryan Routledge and Nicolas Christin, \href{https://doi.org/10.1145/3442381.3450059}{``Towards Understanding Cryptocurrency Derivatives:A Case Study of BitMEX''}}{Research}{Research paper}{Proceedings of the Web Conference 2021 (WWW '21), 45--57 (2021); DOI 10.1145/3442381.3450059.}{Case study of BitMEX, the venue that set the template for settled and perpetual crypto futures with up to 100x leverage. Traces the evolution of its products and uses on-chain forensics, public liquidation events and the venue's chat room to describe its traders, from wealthy automated strategies to small, short-horizon risky positions. Discusses how derivative trading produced sharp moves in spot markets.}{}

\section{Crypto spot markets}\label{catalogue-section-18-spot}
\label{sec:crypto-spot}
Spot trading of bitcoin and other tokens on centralised exchanges, in futures and through exchange-traded products: price discovery and arbitrage, exchange market quality and manipulation, valuation models, return dynamics, investors and access, and exchange failures and regulation. Derivatives on these assets are in \hyperref[catalogue-section-18-1-sub-perpetuals-options-and-crypto-rates]{Perpetuals, options and crypto rates}; cross-sectional factor research is in \hyperref[catalogue-section-18-1-sub-returns-factors-and-allocation]{Returns, factors and allocation}.
\Needspace{8\baselineskip}
\subsection{Price discovery, arbitrage and reference rates}\label{catalogue-section-18-spot-sub-price-discovery}
\label{sec:crypto-spot-discovery}
Which venues lead the price, why cross-exchange arbitrage is limited by settlement latency and counterparty risk, how futures and spot ETFs changed price discovery, and how reference rates are fixed from constituent-exchange trades.

CF Benchmarks is authorised by the UK FCA as a benchmark administrator.}{}

\section{Crypto market making}\label{catalogue-section-18-market-making}
\label{sec:crypto-market-making}
Liquidity provision in crypto markets: order-book microstructure, fees and impact on centralised venues; quoting and execution strategies, learning agents and their backtests; token market makers, listings and enforcement; and liquidity provision on decentralised exchanges, including just-in-time liquidity and fee-tier fragmentation. AMM design and LP returns are in Section~\ref{catalogue-section-18-3}; venue documentation and replay tools are in Sections~\ref{catalogue-section-18-1} and~\ref{catalogue-section-20-1}.

\section{Crypto trading strategies}\label{catalogue-section-18-strategies}
\label{sec:crypto-strategies}
Directional and relative-value strategies on crypto assets, excluding market making: cross-sectional factors and anomalies, trend following, technical rules and calendar effects, statistical arbitrage and pairs trading, arbitrage and DeFi carry, attention, sentiment and event-driven signals, and machine-learning prediction and portfolio allocation. Crypto factor models and on-chain signals are in Section~\ref{catalogue-section-18-1}; perpetual carry in Section~\ref{catalogue-section-18-1}; market making in Section~\ref{catalogue-section-18-market-making}.
\Needspace{8\baselineskip}

Short-term reversal, momentum, and liquidity effects in cryptocurrency markets''}}{Research}{Research paper}{International Review of Financial Analysis, 78, 101908 (2021); DOI 10.1016/j.irfa.2021.101908.}{Shows on more than 3,600 coins that yesterday's return predicts today's in the cross-section: last-day losers beat last-day winners, and the effect survives a battery of controls. The reversal comes from illiquidity, so it fades with liquidity, and the largest, most tradeable coins show daily momentum instead. Reconciles earlier conflicting results on return persistence.}{}

\section{AMMs, lending and liquidity design}\label{catalogue-section-18-3}
\label{sec:s11-topic-4}
\label{sec:exp-amm-frontier}
Read the CFMM and Uniswap v3 foundations first. These works separate passive liquidity exposure, informed-flow losses, fee design and programmable execution; mechanism-design claims remain conditional on the specified protocol and participants. Lending protocols, liquidations and the oracles they depend on follow in their own subsection.

\section{Staking, liquid claims and token economics}\label{catalogue-section-18-4}
\label{sec:depth-digital-staking}
Distinguish native ETH, a validator deposit, a liquid-staking claim, a restaked position, and a protocol governance token. Their rewards, exit rights, loss waterfalls and price exposures are different even when all are quoted in ETH.
\CatalogueEntry{depth-cong-staking-2025}{Lin William Cong, Zhiheng He and Ke Tang, \href{https://www.nber.org/papers/w33640}{The Tokenomics of Staking}}{Research}{Research paper}{NBER Working Paper 33640, April 2025; working paper at the cut-off.}{Models allocation between transactional tokens and staked tokens; staking ratio affects productivity, adoption, reward rate and token price. Its empirical tests separate cross-sectional staking rewards from time-series responses and help frame staking yield as an endogenous network outcome, not a bond coupon. Read after the \hyperlink{s6-cryptofactors}{crypto risk-factor study}. Preserve working-paper status and estimate issuance and fee changes separately.}{\href{catalogue_extended_notes.html\#depth-cong-staking-2025}{Extended note}.}
