\CatalogueEntry{roadmap-yieldspace}{Allan Niemerg, Dan Robinson and Lev Livnev, \href{https://yield.is/YieldSpace.pdf}{YieldSpace: An Automated Liquidity Provider for Fixed Yield Tokens}}{Advanced}{Research paper}{August 2020 working draft, revision 1 (as stated on the paper). Primary PDF inspected 12 October 2026; retain its working-draft status.}{Read the constant power-sum invariant as a curve designed for fixed-yield tokens rather than spot assets. \section{Tokenisation and stablecoin funding}\label{catalogue-section-18-5}

\subsection{Stablecoin pegs, runs and reserve assets}\label{catalogue-section-18-5-sub-stablecoin-stability}
Peg arbitrage and its limits, the design theory of collateralised and algorithmic stablecoins, run evidence from Terra, the 2021 algorithmic runs and the March 2023 USDC depeg, market-implied devaluation risk, and the international standards for stablecoin arrangements.

\section{Tokenised securities and real-world assets}\label{catalogue-section-18-tokenised-assets}
\label{sec:tokenised-assets}
Tokenised versions of existing securities and funds, and tokens that create new fractional claims on ventures, property and unique assets. \chapter{Event contracts and prediction markets}\label{catalogue-chapter-18-events}
\label{sec:exp-prediction-frontier}
Event contracts pay a fixed amount if a stated event happens. The chapter runs from what an event price reveals, through the wagering-market literature on biases and through decision markets, to venues, outcome tokens, resolution, integrity and regulation, and finally to trading: automated and order-book market making, event derivatives and combos, and trading strategies. Exchange-listed, on-chain and bookmaker markets appear side by side: the economics of an event contract does not depend on its settlement layer, but its data, resolution and custody do.
\Needspace{13\baselineskip}
\section{Event prices, beliefs and forecasts}\label{catalogue-section-18-7}
\ExtendedNote{subject-118}{Prediction-market research should incorporate contract resolution rules, oracle and dispute mechanisms, capital lock-up, correlated outcomes, trader wealth constraints, jurisdictional access and event-time liquidity collapse. For decentralised venues, on-chain settlement data should be joined to off-chain order-book data rather than assuming either layer alone gives a complete trading record.}
\href{catalogue_extended_notes.html\#subject-118}{Subject context and qualifications}.
Four subsections: what an event price can reveal; the forecast record; the wagering-market literature on the favourite--longshot bias, bookmakers and exchanges; and decision, corporate and scientific markets.
\Needspace{8\baselineskip}

\section{Event-contract venues, settlement and regulation}\label{catalogue-section-18-ev-venues}
The spot market for event contracts: how outcomes are resolved and paid, how claims are held as fractional or tokenised positions, how the trade record is abused, and how venues are regulated.

\subsection{Outcome tokens, fractional contracts and cross-venue identity}\label{catalogue-section-18-ev-sub-tokens}
\CatalogueEntry{ev-peterson-augur-2015}{Jack Peterson, Joseph Krug, Micah Zoltu, Austin K. Williams and Stephanie Alexander, \href{https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.1501.01042}{``Augur: A Decentralized Oracle and Prediction Market Platform''}}{Advanced}{Research preprint}{White paper, arXiv 1501.01042, v3 (30 November 2020); DOI 10.48550/arXiv.1501.01042.}{Augur white paper: a trustless oracle and prediction-market platform in which holders of the Reputation token stake on observed outcomes for settlement fees. Disputes escalate through growing bonds; past a threshold Reputation forks into one version per outcome, and only the version matching reality should keep value. Read for how a token can underwrite settlement, and why that is costly and slow.}{}

\CatalogueEntry{ev-gebele-matthes-2026-lop}{Jonas Gebele and Florian Matthes, \href{https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2601.01706}{``Semantic Non-Fungibility and Violations of the Law of One Price in Prediction Markets''}}{Research}{Research preprint}{arXiv preprint 2601.01706, v1 (5 January 2026); DOI 10.48550/arXiv.2601.01706.}{The same event listed on different venues is not the same asset: without a shared event identity, liquidity does not pool and arbitrage is costly or unenforceable. In negative-risk events, where only one outcome can win, a NO share in one market converts into a YES share in every other. \section{Event-contract trading: market making, derivatives and strategies}\label{catalogue-section-18-ev-trading}
Who supplies liquidity and how it is priced, from scoring-rule market makers to order books and request-for-quote auctions; contracts built on event prices (binary options, parimutuel auctions, combos and belief-volatility models); and the evidence on trading strategies, arbitrage and stake sizing.

\part{Data, systems and research resources}
\chapter{Data specifications, identifiers and sources}\label{catalogue-chapter-19}
Use identified data specifications and versioned identifiers to reconstruct observations. Product availability, revisions and rights to use data are distinct from economic coverage.
\Needspace{13\baselineskip}
\section{Identifiers, disclosures and trade lifecycles}\label{catalogue-section-19-1}
\label{sec:exp-data-provenance}
Read the source specifications before building a return panel or event replay. Observation time, publication time, revisions, identifiers, corporate actions and trade lifecycle events determine which research claims the data can support.

\section{Data biases, cleaning and vendor documentation}\label{catalogue-section-19-biases}

\chapter{Software and research infrastructure}\label{catalogue-chapter-20}
Software provides reference implementations and infrastructure, not automatic validation. Papers and their implementation repositories retain distinct identities and maintenance conditions.
\Needspace{13\baselineskip}
\section{Libraries, platforms and simulation}\label{catalogue-section-20-1}
\label{sec:codebases}
\ExtendedNote{subject-126}{Software and source-available projects should be judged on deterministic replay, data lineage, test coverage, extensibility, licence, numerical correctness, maintained venue adapters and separation between research convenience and production safety. Repository status and cited release documentation were screened on 4 October 2026; a recent commit, a public repository or an available release does not establish an open-source licence or validated installation. Popularity is not evidence of matching-engine fidelity or institutional suitability. Vectorised daily-bar engines can be useful for preliminary research, but they often conceal order-state, partial-fill, corporate-action, borrow, margin and timestamp assumptions. Similarly, a framework's support for ``live trading'' does not mean it accurately represents co-location, multicast feeds, drop-copy reconciliation, exchange gateways, OTC lifecycle events or institutional controls.}
\href{catalogue_extended_notes.html\#subject-126}{Subject context and qualifications}.

\section{Clearing, settlement and institutional dependencies}\label{catalogue-section-21-2}
\label{sec:exp-institutional-controls}
These are specific institutional references for model oversight, aggregation, funding and market infrastructure. Read them with the model-risk guidance and distinguish general principles, dated policy analysis and jurisdiction-specific implementation material.
\CatalogueEntry{exp-pfmi}{CPSS and IOSCO Technical Committee, \href{https://www.bis.org/cpmi/publ/d101a.pdf}{Principles for Financial Market Infrastructures}}{Advanced}{Contract / specification / guidance}{Final CPSS-IOSCO Principles for financial market infrastructures published 16 April 2012; checked 4 October 2026.}{Framework for payment systems, central securities depositories, settlement systems, central counterparties and trade repositories. Prioritise credit and liquidity risk, collateral, margin, settlement finality, default procedures and operational resilience when studying how a strategy survives participant failure. Clearing transforms and mutualises exposures; it does not remove funding needs or every tail loss. Pair the general principles with the actual CCP rulebook and account structure for a concrete strategy.}{}
